“Also no. You said sincere. If you make me sit an examination about my own head, what exactly will you have measured?”

Dessa looked down at the loose tools arranged on her cloth. Mevia’s objection was mechanically sound, which was inconvenient.

“Just turn it,” Lutik said. He was checking the window light against a pocket watch. “Whatever happens, do it quickly.”

Mevia took the key. “You may look. You may not comment on the furniture.”

“Mevia,” Sikra began.

The key turned.

Warmth breathed into the room, rich with yeast, scorched sugar, and orange peel. The doorway opened onto a small sitting room under sloped rafters. A green shawl lay over the arm of a chair beside two cups and a bowl of walnuts. Notes had been tucked around the edge of a wall mirror. A string hung from the ceiling with little paper stars folded along it, each one turning in the draft from the door.

A woman in a red apron looked up from a saucepan on a narrow stove. Surprise crossed her face, followed by recognition that did not include the people behind Mevia.

“You said after supper,” she said.

“The repair finished early.” Mevia shifted sideways, blocking most of the frame. Her voice changed, not softer exactly, but relieved of the little edge it had used in the old house. “Is the syrup all right?”

“It will be if I stop staring at your aunt.”

Lutik coughed into his fist. Sikra looked as though an unfamiliar law had been passed in her absence.

“We are testing,” Mevia said. “We are not visiting.”

The woman in the apron nodded once. “Then close it before the buns sink.”

Mevia stepped back and pulled the door shut. The paper stars spun once above her head and vanished. A tuft of flour drifted down into the tray.

Jorren rubbed it between thumb and forefinger. “Rooms over a shop.”

“Bakery,” Mevia said.

“You rent them.”

“Reliably.”

“That doesn’t make them—”

“Do not finish that sentence while eating her wife’s buns,” Lutik said.

The smell of orange peel lingered in the stripped room. Mevia brushed flour from her sleeve and sat. She did not explain the second cup, the stars, or the voice her wife had used. She had permitted a threshold, not a tour.

Sikra turned to Dessa. “Can you bias it?”

“Toward what?”

Sikra pointed down again. “This house. The family address in the deed.”

There were fixed-route gates built for that purpose. They used dead geometry, calibrated ends, and enough silver wire to make theft worth worrying about. A recognition door was older and stranger. Its central rail had been filed over generations into a shape no diagram could restore once lost.

“I could remove the recognition core and fit a fixed route,” Dessa said. “Not today, and not without rebuilding both stiles. It would no longer be this kind of door. The old rail might not survive removal.”

“You repaired it to go elsewhere.”

“I repaired the split in the rail and the swollen latch. I haven’t changed what selects the route.”

Sikra pressed her fingertips to the black ribbon on her cuff. “When my mother had it, we all came through here.”

“When your mother had it,” Lutik said, “most of us lived here.”

Sikra gave him a look that would have stopped a lesser current.

Dessa concentrated on the lock. She restored the new spring, returned the hinge pins to their original direction, and checked every measurement twice. Part of her still hoped that the next turn would reveal a loose tooth, an intermittent contact, anything that could be corrected without choosing what to destroy. Her fee mattered. So did the message her master would receive before morning: first solo traveling repair, client claims four destinations. But beneath both worries lay the rail itself, warm as skin after every use, carrying a century of minute file marks. She would not cut it into obedience because the room preferred one answer.

“One final neutral test,” she said. “No prompting. No adjustment after.”

Jorren had already stood. He looked less reluctant now. “Give me the key.”

Sikra did. “Think clearly.”

“I am.”

He turned it hard enough that the bow struck the plate.

The opening revealed a blue-tiled kitchen. A pot soaked in the basin. A pair of gardening gloves lay on the table beside an unopened letter, and a tall plant leaned toward a window silvered by evening. Nothing in the room was grand. Nothing looked temporary.

Jorren’s whole face changed. Hope did not improve it. It made him look younger and more dangerous to himself.

“See?” he said. “I told you.”

A figure entered the kitchen, stopped, and gripped the back of a chair.

“Jorren.”

He put one foot on the sill. “The door brought me.”

“Take your foot back.”

“It knows where I belong.”

The figure crossed the kitchen. Dessa saw a drawn face, a work shirt with one cuff unfastened, and no welcome in either. “I told you not to come without asking.”

“This is asking.”

“No. This is arriving.”

Jorren leaned into the threshold. The other person seized the inner handle. For an instant they held the same door from opposite sides, one pulling, one resisting. The catch strap shivered. Dessa’s tools jumped against one another on the floor.

“Let go,” Dessa said.

Neither did.

She drove the service wedge under the near corner with the heel of her hand. The leaf lifted just enough to break Jorren’s leverage. The person in the kitchen pulled it closed. The latch entered the strike without scrape or bounce.

Then came the blunt slide of an ordinary bolt on the destination side.

Jorren twisted the handle. It moved a finger’s breadth and stopped. He looked at Dessa. “Open it.”

She was already kneeling, one palm on the brass strip. The current had run true. The repaired latch carried the load evenly against its spring. Beyond it, the local bolt sat in its keeper. Plain hardware, doing its plain job.

“You have picks,” Jorren said.

“For locks I’m authorized to service.”

“My things are in that house.”

“Then arrange to collect them.”

“The door says it’s my home.”

Dessa withdrew her hand from the brass. Around them, the stripped room had gone still. Even Sikra no longer paced.

“The door opened where you recognize home,” Dessa said. “The bolt belongs to the person on the other side.”

Jorren stared at her as if waiting for the rest, some locksmith’s exception hidden behind those two facts.

There was none.

He yanked the handle once more. The frame held. Then he released it and stepped away, his anger searching the room for an easier object. Nobody offered one.

Dessa removed the wedge. She opened her service ledger on the nearest chair and wrote while the results were fresh.

*User one: local destination; current clean; latch seated.*

She paused over the word *local*, remembering Sikra stepping through the frame to stand in the same room. It had seemed like no travel because there had been no distance to cross.

*User two: moving domestic berth; stable route under motion and weather.*

Lutik glanced again at his watch, but he had stopped talking about the tide.

*User three: occupied rented rooms; stable route; destination notified.*

Mevia’s eyes narrowed at that last phrase. “Write ‘invited.’ She knew about the test.”

Dessa amended it.

*User four: occupied household; stable route; entry refused by destination-side bolt.*

Four turns. Four centered strikes. No wandering, no heat in the key, no slip in the rail. Each opening had held until somebody shut it.

At the bottom she wrote: *Repair complete. Recognition core retained.*

Sikra read over her shoulder. “You call this complete?”

Dessa’s stomach tightened, but her voice did not. “Yes.”

“I hired you so they could return here.”

“You hired me to restore the traveling door.”

“A careful distinction.”

“Locks are made of them.”

Lutik gave a tired snort. Mevia hid hers badly. Jorren stood at the window, apart from the rest.

Sikra did not smile. She took the coin purse from her skirt pocket, weighed it in her palm, and set it beside Dessa’s tool roll. “You will give me a copy of those results.”

“Without the descriptions of private rooms.”

“Without those,” Sikra agreed after a moment.

Dessa packed the reversed pins, the worn spring, her gauges and pots of paste. Behind her, the family’s argument resumed, but its shape had changed.

“The boat can take the frame as far as the lower crossings,” Lutik said. “Not before next week.”

“It is not living on your boat,” Sikra said.

“There isn’t room for it,” he said, which was not quite the same answer.

Mevia offered dry storage above the bakery if everyone promised to send notice before using it. Sikra objected to asking permission to visit her own niece. Mevia replied that notice was not permission, though sometimes permission would also be required. Jorren said nothing until Sikra began assigning days to clear the upstairs. Then he said he could manage the heavy wardrobes on fifth-day, provided they used a cart and the ordinary road.

No one chose where the door would stand. They agreed on two clearing days, disagreed about remembrance supper, and began a fresh quarrel over whether the copper tray counted as part of the inheritance.

Dessa buckled her repair case. Last, she removed the service wedge from beneath the oak and slipped it into its loop. The door stood square without her hand on it.

She left the family measuring the frame and speaking, with unfamiliar care, about who would knock first. At the front entrance she chose the house’s ordinary brass latch and went down the stone steps with the coin purse knocking inside her repair case.

stories.title: The Shadow That Nested
stories.prompt: A moon begins casting two shadows across the world below. An orbital repair crew discovers that the second shadow comes from an ancient sunshade mistaken for a celestial omen—and that an enormous living migration has built its nests across the machinery needed to move it.
stories.body:
# The Shadow That Nested

The moon's night crosses the world first. From the repair tug, Oru Pendrothiel watches its round umbra pass over white cloud and the copper shine of an ocean, exactly where the orbit model promised.

Nine minutes later, darkness crosses again.

The second track has a straight leading edge and a ragged tail. It extinguishes the tops of daylight storms, then runs out over the ocean. Surface feeds arrive crowded with explanations: a celestial warning, a second moon too dark to see, a wing folded over the sun. Oru discards messages without timestamps. The rest agree within four seconds.

Beside him, Nemi Quell folds the thermal returns through the moon's orbital plane. "The trailing edge loses heat in strips. Twelve of them, overlapping."

"Range the source, not the surface."

"I need us thirty kilometers higher to separate it from the moon."

Oru changes the tug's climb. "Match the unknown's angular rate. Keep six meters per second in hand."

The new trajectory spends part of their maneuver margin. It also brings the thing out from behind the moon before the next surface crossing.

Stars vanish ahead. As the tug rises, darkness resolves into a black disk canted nearly edge-on to the sun, twelve flexible petals around a thick hub. One petal has warped toward its neighbor. Dust on the immense outer rim forces the scanner to assemble its circle piece by piece.

Oru overlays the second shadow. The ragged track fits the overlapping petals. The straight edge fits the one sector that has turned too far toward the world.

"Working name: sunshade," Nemi says. The thermal image shows old heat trapped in the petal laminates and a colder circle at the rim.

"Function unknown. Shadow source confirmed." Oru sends the surface network a position and closes the incoming interpretations. "Next umbra in seven hours, forty-one minutes. Range the hub."

Nothing identifies the builders. The hub offers no beacon or legible record, only layered repairs: clamps over welds, pale ceramic stitched across black membrane, service marks cut through older marks. Whatever the disk once shaded, its present yaw is a hazard. Another three tenths of a degree will broaden the next second night across the same inhabited latitudes.

They dock against a flange beneath mineral crust. When Oru powers its contacts, a diagram wakes in amber lines. Twelve arcuate rails divide the outer ring, each holding a carriage linked inward to a petal edge. Together, the carriages walk the rim around the hub and turn the disk without concentrating force at its brittle center. Oru calls the carriage-and-drive assemblies walkers; the diagram offers no surviving word.

A bright reference line stands beyond the current position. Oru names it zero. The machine's meaning for it is gone; the geometry remains. At zero the disk would lie edge-on to the sun and its shadow would collapse. On younger machines, he does not leave until service and live lines overlap; that habit keeps hidden load from passing to the next crew.

"All twelve brakes report closed," he says. "Links carry load. I can take up slack without travel."

Nemi attaches their sensor bridge to the old ring diagram. "Limit preload to four tenths of nominal. I want each sector separately."

"Four tenths. No brake release."

Oru touches the reset control. Power reaches all twelve tension links in a quick sequence. Eleven strain traces rise with the hard response of metal and laminate.

Sector one's trace keeps rising after its command ends.

"Sector one has a delayed return," Nemi says. "Soft load, seven to eleven kilograms. Cut power."

Oru isolates the ring. The last trace subsides in small elastic steps.

"No carriage displacement," he says.

"Then the load stretched in place. I need the rail open before another test."

They go out through the tug's lock with the sun at their backs.

At orbital distance the shade looks almost flat. Up close, it is folded membrane, hollow trusses, and rail wells wide enough to crawl through. Oru anchors his waist tether to the hub line and a second line to his tool tray. The unpowered skin carries a faint charge; his loose driver inches across its magnetic pad until the tether catches it.

Walker one sits where the first rail meets a petal seam. Its cover has fused around three fasteners. Oru cuts the heads and lifts the plate while Nemi holds a probe against the tension link. The plate rises a finger's width and stops against something springy.

Silver-gray fiber fills the rail well. It loops between the runner's teeth, crosses the spindle, and gathers around the tension link in a sealed bulb larger than Oru's torso. His lamp reveals another bulb under the next cover, then more along the curve, packed wherever the ring offers shelter.

Nemi presses the probe to the sealed mass. "Outer fiber is at rail temperature. The center is warmer by one point six. Heat rises, rests, rises again."

"Runner obstructed. Central reset stays isolated."

"The heat rhythm has a weak electrical edge. It is coupling into the skin. This housing is occupied, and the spindle passes through it."

A faint rasp enters Oru's helmet. His suit returns the end of Nemi's last word several seconds late: through it, it, it. The repetition comes through the tether and shade skin, not across open radio. On his tray the driver creeps again.

Oru clips every tool to a hard line. "Map the warm mass around the ring."

Nemi sends a low pulse through the probes. Warm knots appear by the hundreds, then by the thousands, following all twelve rails. The signal says nothing about what they are. It only makes the machine's supposedly empty spaces visible.

The sunlight dims.

A narrow body passes between Oru and the star, surrounded by six transparent vanes larger than the tug. Blue currents travel through the tissue as it spreads against the light. Another follows, then a procession of dark bodies and flashing vane edges. They miss the shade and angle along the ring. Nemi labels the returns driftwings only to separate them from the sealed nests on the map.

"Adults are crossing the rim," Nemi says. "No size range yet."

"Keep the scanner off their path. We have enough evidence."

Back at the hub, Oru models the available forces without moving anything. A central-clamp tow puts the innermost membrane root at nine times permitted shear; the oldest patch would split before half the required turn. A central reset distributes force, but every runner and spindle would close through warm fiber. Drifting adds another tenth of a degree before the next pass and brings the warped petals into overlap within two passes.

"Direct tow tears petal four at sixty percent of required torque," Oru says. "Central drive damages every occupied rail. Waiting loses the membrane."

Nemi changes the life map from points to bands. "A root tear crosses sectors three through six. The warm nests there are anchored to the laminate; they go with it."

"Can you clear individual walkers?"

"Not through covers. I can clear runner path, spindle core, local heat, and strain response if you seat the probe on each housing before touching its brake."

"Then we inspect clockwise."

"The occupied fraction is between seventy and ninety-four percent. At that density, individual inspection extends past the next umbra."

Oru looks through the hub's open truss. Sunlight has begun to touch walker one. "Measure what warming changes."

They return to the rim and wait beside the first sealed bulb. The shade's slow yaw carries the sunlight across it. At a threshold Nemi cannot yet bound, the silver fibers contract. A seam opens.

A small body pushes free. Its wet-looking vanes spread into six trembling sheets, and sunlight runs blue through them. It remains attached for half a minute before the last filament parts. Two more follow. An adult crosses above, strips a loose ribbon from the shell, and carries it out of Oru's light.

Along the rim, other nests open as the thermal line reaches them. The openings proceed clockwise. Behind that moving boundary, loose fibers lift away from runner teeth and spindle gaps. Ahead of it, the woven bulbs remain closed and warm.

Nemi works the probe over the first exposed mechanism. "Runner path has no attached fiber. Spindle has no internal heat rhythm. Skin temperature is falling toward bare rail. Strain return is metallic."

"One is the local test stroke."

"One is clear within sensor range. I have no clearance for the next housing."

Oru studies the moving strip of empty machinery. It is narrow, but it is going where the disk must turn.

"We stay behind the boundary," he says. "I traverse the rim and seat the probe. You return to the hub and read each housing. Local manual pulses only."

Nemi marks four abort lines on his wrist display. "Runner obstruction, spindle rhythm, heat above bare-skin range, or soft strain return. Any one stops the stroke."

"Call all four before brake release."

"The echoes are delayed up to three seconds."

Oru hears seconds arrive again from the shade. "End each clearance with the walker number. I answer with number and state. Old words carry the wrong number."

Nemi clips the multipoint probe to his tool rail and waits for the echo to die. "That is sufficient. Keep every tool tethered." Then they push off toward the hub.

At walker one, Oru seats the probe and a hand controller directly into the carriage. The cleared wake extends only twenty meters clockwise. Beyond it, the next closed nests shine like bundled wire.

Nemi's voice comes from the hub. "Runner open. Spindle cold. Heat within two tenths of bare rail. Strain hard-return. One."

"One releasing."

He trips the brake, gives the controller a short pulse, and feels the ring move through his boots. The carriage advances along its arc; the tension link draws the first petal edge sideways. Oru stops at the calculated mark and drives the mechanical lock home.

"One moved and locked."

The orbit overlay on his wrist redraws. The coming umbra shifts eight kilometers toward the world's limb.

Walker two has a brake crusted with mineral growth. Oru wraps it in the waste-heat line from his cutter. Nemi withholds clearance when the spindle temperature rises.

"Heat is climbing with your tool. No occupancy rhythm detected. Hold until it returns within three tenths. Two."

"Two held. Heater off."

The lost minute lets the hatching boundary pull farther ahead. When the housing cools, Nemi clears each element, and Oru breaks the brake free. The second petal responds more sharply than the first. He shortens the pulse and locks it before their strain ceiling.

At three, the runner is exposed but a newly emerged animal remains tied across the spindle by one bright filament. Oru can see empty space behind its folded vanes. Nemi still says, "Runner open. Spindle obstructed. Heat source moving. No stroke. Three."

Oru retracts the controller. The animal turns in the light without any sign that it sees him. Its filament thins, snaps, and drifts clear. Only after Nemi's probe loses the pulse does Oru release three.

The weak current in a dense cluster ahead sends the ends of Nemi's words back through his radio. At four, an echoed clear arrives after Nemi has found fresh fiber under the runner. The walker number attached to the old word prevents Oru's thumb from arming the drive.

"Four runner obstructed," Nemi says. "Cold loose strand, no coupled heat. Remove from the tooth path; do not pull toward the spindle. Four."

Oru hooks the strand from its free end and folds it beneath the opened cover. Static tugs the hook sideways; its tether snaps straight. Nemi repeats the four-part check, and Oru moves the carriage.

Walker five accepts its first pulse, then the tension link answers too slowly.

"Soft strain return at the lower anchor," Nemi says. "Stop five."

"Five stopped. Brake closing."

The carriage has moved a third of its planned travel. Oru locks it there. The hatch front continues clockwise while Nemi compares the response against the thermal map.

"No heat at the anchor," they say. "Likely old laminate separation, confidence sixty-eight. Five can remain at current position. Reduce later walker strokes by eight percent or the next link inherits the load."

"Eight percent reduction entered. Five stays locked."

The change leaves more shadow for the tug to remove later. It keeps the petal attached now.

Six spreads tension without another soft return and locks cleanly. At seven, a vast driftwing's blue-lit vane fills Oru's visor and blinds the probe's optical channel. Nemi calls the lost heat data; Oru holds the released brake until the animal passes, then pulses and locks seven. At eight, his tether reaches its last guide. He anchors a new line before opening the brake. The old guide bends when the petal moves; eight reaches its reduced mark and locks.

By walker nine, Oru's suit is radiating more heat than the empty nests. Nemi narrows the probe field to separate him from the spindle.

"Move your left boot off the housing. Nine."

Oru shifts to the rail lip. "Boot clear."

"Runner open. Spindle cold. Heat source now external and receding. Strain hard-return. Nine."

"Nine moving."

The echo gives him moving after the lock is already seated.

Walker ten lies beside an ancient patch whose edge rises as the carriage takes load. Nemi calls strain at the patch root rather than at the runner. Oru divides the reduced stroke into three manual pulses, waiting between them for the laminate to flatten, then locks ten beneath the patch. The predicted umbra touches only a narrowing crescent of the world now, but it still reaches the atmosphere.

The nest at eleven opens while Oru approaches. Four young bodies lift into the sunlit stream. Their empty casing collapses around the tension link instead of peeling away. Nemi finds no warmth in it, yet the link cannot move with the loops drawn tight.

"Eleven runner clear. Spindle clear. Heat matches rail. Strain blocked by cast fiber. Mechanical obstruction only. Eleven."

"Eleven brake stays closed. I am clearing the link."

Oru works the loose loops over the end of the housing one at a time. He does not cut until each length lies free of the spindle; then he severs the cold outer web and binds it under the cover.

"Heat unchanged. Strain return is hard. Eleven."

When Oru finally pulses the carriage, the whole shade shudders. A shallow crease runs inward across one petal and fades before reaching the hub.

"Root strain peaked four point one," Nemi says. "Current stable band ends at four point four. No further local stroke there."

"Eleven at mark. Lock engaged."

"Lock load confirmed."

On the old diagram, eleven carriages now sit displaced and mechanically locked. Only walker twelve remains at its starting position. The bright zero line waits beyond it.

Oru follows the empty wake to the last housing. Sunlight has crossed the outer fibers, but the nest has not opened. Tight gray weave encloses the spindle; no vane stirs beneath it. The thermal boundary has passed twelve and continues clockwise across the woven rail. The genuinely cleared wake ends here.

His wrist shows twelve minutes until the shade's umbra begins to touch the high atmosphere.

"Twelve surface is at bare-rail temperature," Oru says. He seats the release tool without turning it. "No motion. Preparing spindle clearance."

"Keep torque at zero," Nemi says. "Put the probe on the anti-sun seam, under the tension link. Six centimeters inward. Twelve."

Oru moves the probe. The suit channel fills with static, then gives back the last syllable of inward again and again. He braces his hand so tool creep cannot turn the release.

"Nothing above noise."

"I have a rise of four hundredths. Seventeen-second interval. Hold for three cycles."

The three cycles cost fifty-one seconds. The machine's reference line stays bright. Oru could release the walker in less than one minute and put the shade where its surviving diagram says it belongs.

Nemi speaks after the third interval. "The rise repeats within one hundredth. Core stays warmer than the outer weave. Occupancy confidence eighty-six to ninety-two. Spindle is not clear. Twelve."

Oru draws the release tool straight out. The spindle remains locked.

"Time to likely opening?"

"No bounded estimate. The surrounding nests opened across a nine-degree heat range. This one is inside that range and still cycling."

"Waiting one pass consumes the shadow window. Bound the occupied sectors under current yaw."

"Petal overlap begins within one to three passes. A tear would cross occupied sectors. I cannot clear waiting as a stable condition."

Oru opens the surface model over the ancient diagram. Zero demands another seven tenths of a degree and twelve's full stroke. The mission demand is smaller. Eleven changed petals have pushed the umbra almost off the world; its inner edge still cuts sixty-two kilometers into the high atmosphere. Another two tenths will clear the model's uncertainty.

The tug can supply that fraction through the hub. It cannot restore zero without tearing the membrane, and an off-center pull will load the locked petals unevenly. Oru reads the fuel figures twice. Forty-three point seven meters per second remain in the tanks. A fast return needs thirty-seven. The shade burn will use as much as sixteen point four. A slow three-loop return needs twenty-four point eight.

"Nemi, isolate drive power to twelve. Keep its mechanical brake set. Verify locks one through eleven."

"One through eleven locked. Twelve drive isolated. The nest rhythm persists."

"Move to the tug controls. We torque the hub clockwise for two tenths. Eleven locks carry the shifted rim; twelve does not stroke."

"The off-center load puts petal four and the tension link at twelve outside tested balance. My strain range widens under thrust."

"Set abort at four point four root strain, nest warming three tenths, or fuel twenty-seven. Minimum umbra clearance is twelve kilometers."

Nemi does not answer until their route marker begins moving from the hub toward the docked tug. "Recoil can add two tenths after cutoff. Lower the thrust ceiling nine percent and cut at four point two."

"Ceiling reduced nine. Strain cutoff four point two. Heat and fuel cutoffs unchanged."

"Then modeled warming stays inside the observed heat range if the link holds. I will call lower-bound umbra clearance, not center track."

"Use tank value with every burn command. Ignore echoes without a current value."

Nemi reaches the tug. "Ready at forty-three point seven."

Oru anchors both tethers beside twelve and braces one boot on each side of its rail. He can see the nest, its outer tension link, and the root of petal four across the disk. Beyond them, the bright curve of the world enters the moon's approaching shadow.

"Start at forty-three point seven," he says.

The tug's lateral thrusters fire while its clamps hold the hub. Torque travels outward along the petal roots. Eleven displaced walkers take it through their locked carriages. Because the twelfth carriage remains at its original rail position, that sector lags elastically and the disk cups around Oru.

His waist line pulls toward the hub. The nest does not move relative to its spindle, but the tension link bows beneath it.

"Root strain three point six and rising," Nemi says. "Nest rhythm present. Fuel forty-one point nine."

"Reduce thrust four percent. Hold vector."

The thrust softens. A crease in petal four points toward Oru, then stops lengthening. Abandoned fibers rise from the eleven cleared sectors. Driftwing adults follow the hatching boundary, vanes opening and closing in sunlight. Nest pulses coupling into the skin return the old word hold after the actual command is over.

The orbit model crawls across his wrist. The shade's umbra retreats toward the world's edge.

"Lower-bound penetration thirty-eight kilometers," Nemi says. "Root strain three point nine. Twelve core warmer by seven hundredths. Fuel thirty-eight point six."

"Continue. Same ceiling."

A lock at sector six skips one tooth. Oru feels the impact through the rim before the diagram marks it. The recoil rotates him against his tether and loads the twelve link sideways.

"Six slipped. Cut thrust to half at thirty-seven point eight."

"Half thrust, thirty-seven point eight."

The old echo repeats eight while Nemi's measured fuel falls past it. Oru watches sector six settle against its second tooth. Petal four's crease shortens by a handspan.

"Six holding on secondary tooth," he says. "Raise to three quarters. Cap strain four point two."

"Three quarters. Cap four point two. Fuel thirty-six point nine."

The direct return has vanished from the route display. In its place, the tug draws a long falling loop around the moon and two slower loops before meeting the world. The available margin shrinks with every second of thrust.

The shade turns another fraction. The second umbra reaches the bright atmospheric rim and becomes a narrow blade laid against it.

"Lower bound minus nine kilometers," Nemi says. "Root four point one. Nest warming one tenth. Fuel thirty-two point four."

"Continue to plus twelve or abort."

The membrane's vibration passes through Oru's boots and ribs. The closed nest presses against the bowed link. Under his glove, its faint rhythm comes once, disappears in the structural tremor, then comes again.

"Lower bound plus four. Fuel thirty point one."

"Continue."

"Plus nine. Root four point one nine."

"Reduce to quarter. Cut on the next lower-bound clearance."

The tug's thrust falls. The heavy disk keeps turning under its own flex, returning some of the strain it has stored. Oru's wrist trace crosses the target.

"Lower bound plus thirteen kilometers," Nemi says. "Root four point two. Fuel twenty-nine point three. Nest warming one tenth."

"Cut at twenty-nine point three."

The thrusters stop.

Asymmetric recoil runs around the ring. Walker six strikes its lock. Petal four flattens, overshoots, and cups the other way. Oru's tethers pull tight enough to force air from his lungs, but twelve's brake does not release. The closed nest stays wrapped around the unmoved spindle.

On his wrist, the current shade umbra passes thirteen kilometers beyond the atmosphere at the lower edge of the prediction range. Only the moon's darkness touches the world.

Oru keeps his glove on the nest while the structure settles. The warm core rises by four hundredths, falls, and rises again after seventeen seconds.

"Rhythm remains inside the preburn band," Nemi says. "Root strain is three point seven and falling. Eleven locks hold. Twelve is fixed."

"Keep the ring isolated. Open the slow return solution."

Oru waits until the next heat rise before leaving the rail. The ancient display still shows every carriage short of its zero mark. Petal four retains a shallow off-center fold, and the locked walkers carry loads no surviving diagram calls normal.

At the hub, he closes the local service covers without sealing the nest housings. The tug undocks with twenty-nine point one meters per second in its tanks. Nemi commits them to the first long loop, twenty-four point eight reserved for the eventual descent and capture.

The crooked shade diminishes behind the moon. Its predicted umbra keeps clear of the world for the current alignment. On Oru's wrist, the sensor at walker twelve records another small rise of heat as the tug begins its slow, low-fuel return.

stories.title: The Count Was 131,072
stories.prompt: The museum's new wing commemorates the ancient Battle of the Bay: one queen, alone, against an invasion the plaques round to "countless." You have read every caption. The count was 131,072. She never carried a sword. And the audio guide keeps mispronouncing your name. (Solstice Evening Bell, centuries on — memory-versus-myth with the last living witness as its own subject.)
stories.body:
# The Count Was 131,072

The audio bead says your name wrong before you have properly entered the new wing.

“Sol-*steece* Evening Bell,” it murmurs into the thumb-width field of air behind your right ear, “stood alone against countless invaders in what became known as the Battle of the Bay.”

You stop with one foot inside the painted slow lane. The visitor behind you raises two fingers to her collar, the common sign for *listening*, and steps around without looking annoyed. Museum manners have survived better than royal ones.

The correct first syllable is already in the machine. It is the second that has been sharpened into something foreign and grand. You touch the bead clipped below your ear, discover no pronunciation control, and let the track continue.

You came to read every caption before deciding whether to answer any of them. A bad vowel does not release you from the promise.

The entrance hall is built around your silhouette.

It rises through two stories of smoked glass: crown streaming like a small sun, skirts driven backward by an impossible wind, one arm extended toward a black seam in the sky. The other hand grips a sword as tall as you are. Through the glass, small figures cross the pale floor beneath your feet and disappear into your hem.

You never carried a sword.

There were girls in some circles who did. There were spears, knives, ribbons hardened to edges, a bronze pestle once used with terrible efficiency. Your own hands had other work. A sword would have occupied one.

The plaque calls it an “artist’s synthesis of surviving battle imagery.” The images are not from the battle. The offshore cameras failed when the host descended, the military feeds show weather and interference, and the clearest surviving picture of you was taken years earlier at a ceremony where someone else’s blade happened to stand behind your shoulder. The artist has been careful with the boots and invented everything above them.

Then comes the word in raised silver letters large enough to read from the stairs:

**COUNTLESS.**

The count was 131,072.

Eight wedges emerged through the stationary rupture, 16,384 frames to a wedge. They were not soldiers. They did not fear, surrender, choose, or mourn. Roughly human-sized shells unfolded vanes in the upper dark and arranged themselves around pulses that your crown could hear. A living army might have become countless through panic: bodies crossing, breaking, hiding, returning. These kept their places.

You kept them too.

Track Two wakes when you approach the count wall.

“Although later legends assign precise totals to the enemy, contemporary instruments could not penetrate the storm. Most historians therefore describe the force faced by Sol-*steece* Evening Bell as effectively countless.”

The wall displays eight fan-shaped clouds of light. Their dots drift so that no visitor can hold one arrangement long enough to reckon it. A child has planted both hands on the glass and is trying anyway, counting in fierce whispers until a programmed gust scatters the formation. His adult says, “It means there were too many.”

It means the designer thought motion looked more frightening than arithmetic.

Your count began at the rupture, twenty kilometers over the water. Royal hearing did not sound like bells despite the name later historians gave it. It was pressure without air, interval without music: mass and position held against your nerves, each frame a point in a structure too large for sight. The mesh threw false pulses. You learned their hollowness. The frames changed formation. You changed the shape in which you remembered them.

The first full chord removed 32,768. The absence opened in your hearing before the wreckage began to fall, the leading quarter cut from each of all eight wedges, leaving 98,304.

The same chord, used again, destroyed fewer than a hundred.

The wall skips that. Its next panel shows the glass queen discovering a brighter sword.

You lean close enough to read the small caption beneath the animation. It praises “a decisive second strike.” No number is offered. The host had learned the shape of the first blow and passed it through the mesh; repetition had become almost useless. That was the first honest thing it taught you. Not terror. Not resolve. The cost of admiring your own solution.

A family crosses the threshold too quickly, and three beads trigger at once. For a moment the air fills with private voices leaking at their edges—your wrong name, directions to the accessible lift, a request not to touch the wall. Everyone involved lifts two fingers to a collar. The family backs into the blue slow lane, laughing softly, and their tracks separate.

Your guide resumes as if it has never been interrupted.

“The queen’s legendary weapon may have changed form as the battle demanded.”

“No,” you tell it.

The bead is only a speaker. It neither hears nor fails to hear you.

The crown case occupies the next room. Here the museum lowers its lights and its voice. A silver replica hangs above black velvet, twelve chimes orbiting a larger central bell. The proportions are close. Whoever made it had studied the ceremonial portraits and noticed that the third tone hung a finger-width lower than the ninth. Whoever wrote the label had not shown the same care.

**THE TWELVE WITHIN**

According to the plaque, twelve dead warriors endured as spirits bound to the First Monarch’s crown, lending their strength in battle until their final sacrifice set them free.

You read it twice. You have read every prior caption twice as well, but this time the second reading is not for accuracy. It is to keep your hands at your sides.

They did not endure inside anything.

Twelve adults made twelve final works. Each knew the compact. Each chose while choice still belonged to them, and the act of making was fatal. Their minds did not enter the silver. Their souls went where the dead had always gone. What remained with you was shaped power without appetite or voice, a spell incapable of so much as a spark until your living nerves woke it.

You remember the people. That is different.

The museum would like their names. An inset screen invites visitors to explore “the lost identities of the Twelve,” assembling candidates from folktales, court lists, and graves damaged past certainty. Two guesses are people you knew. Neither donated a spell. One donor appears in the list under a title she despised.

Your memories could settle some of this. A date at a bedside. A joke made badly because there was no good way to ask one final time. The precise pressure of a hand that had gone cold before you understood you were still holding it. None of those things are required to correct the case. You do not owe them to the glass.

On the far side, a child-sized handle lets visitors “play the crown.” Turning it lights each replica chime and adds a tone to a pleasant chord. The mechanism sticks at seven. A museum attendant is nowhere in sight, so you turn it backward, slowly, until the gears release. The next visitor reaches twelve and grins at the harmony.

It is not the chord. It is better for a room full of children.

The central gallery begins with a warning about storms and battle sound. You step onto a circular floor painted as the Bay. The northern breakwater lies under one boot, the southern beneath the other; the eastern ridge curves at the room’s edge. Above, the rupture is a dark ring in the dome.

The reconstruction puts your glass double on the shore.

Of course it does. A queen in the sky would be hard to see, and a queen twenty kilometers below her enemy cannot meet its gaze. The projection plants its feet between the breakwaters. Music gathers. One hundred thousand black figures pour down the dome in a quantity made impressive by refusing to number it.

Your double draws the sword.

You know what follows. The blade will enlarge into a column of gold. It will pass upward once. Every black figure will fall. The twelve captive spirits will fly free as women made of light, young and grateful, and the queen will remain alone in a clean dawn.

The spectacle is beautiful.

That is its worst defense and its best one. Gold trembles across the painted water. The score finds a low note that visitors feel through their shoes. People tilt their faces toward your double with open delight. For eleven minutes the room gives them weather, danger, sacrifice, and survival, each event waiting politely for the last to finish.

Your battle had no such manners.

You moved between sounding chimes on straight routes while the host tried to close around them. Edict planes held where two tones could still answer each other. Needles hissed through rain. Frames struck at speeds that turned correction into impact. After the first three tones burned, 49,152 points remained at the tropopause, and the gaps in royal hearing hurt more than the wounds you could place in your body.

You do not remember each destroyed frame. You remember the structure reducing. Six more tones. Storm winds no spell commanded. Landing geometries narrowed by breakwater, shelf, and ridge. Eight columns of 1,024. Then the last three orbiting tones, spent to destroy four columns and crush the survivors together.

When royal hearing vanished with the twelfth, the world did not become silent. The storm remained. Your own pulse remained. Four thousand ninety-six synchronized frames descended beyond the reach of the faculty that had let you place every one of the original host.

There was no sword stroke. You closed the circuit through your living body, the dying trails of twelve ruined works, and the invasion lattice. Then you crushed the central resonator.

Your crown did not free anyone. It ceased to exist.

The projection’s blade rises.

Force still answers you, centuries later: immense, unharmonized, less exact than what you spent but entirely yours. You could cut one bright seam through the false sword without warming the hands of the visitors below it. You could interrupt the sound system, scar the projection surface, leave an error no conservator could politely attribute to age.

Every face in the room would turn toward a solitary queen performing power beneath her own enormous image.

You watch the sword fall instead.

The projected spirits ascend. The audience applauds—not loudly, not as if at a theater, but with the uncertain little patter people use when an exhibit has moved them and no one knows whether appreciation is permitted. You do not blame them. The ridge did survive. The rupture did close. No second wave came through. The exhibit has taken two true things and built a sword between them.

Track Five says, “Sol-*steece* Evening Bell’s victory marked the beginning of—”

You step out before hearing what it began.

The shore archive is quieter. No monumental glass, no music underfoot. Its first case contains evacuation orders, route maps, transport tallies, maintenance calls, and copies of messages sent by people who never saw what fought above them. These records are offered as context. The type is small. Several visitors glance in and continue toward the interactive memorial at the exit.

You begin at the left edge and read.

A harbor dispatcher recorded the emptied roads as an operational hazard: without ordinary traffic noise, crews kept mistaking loose signs for approaching vehicles. A transport driver reported clearing the eastern ridge before the rupture widened, then complained that the passengers would not stay seated because the storm made the road lights flicker. A weather observer wrote that the clouds appeared to pulse from within. Someone sheltering inland insisted the battle sounded like furniture being dragged across an upstairs room.

You remember none of this.

The people who wrote these records have been dead for centuries. Their copies sit under glass; you stand outside it. That difference is why the wing calls you the last living witness. It does not give you their roads.

From twenty kilometers up, there had been no empty-road quiet. Royal hearing held the host; ordinary hearing caught wind, impacts, your own teeth meeting when a frame changed direction too late. You did not see the last transport pass the ridge. You had been counting the seventh wedge and testing a false pulse. You cannot say whether the passengers stood. You cannot say what the sky looked like from below.

The observation is obvious enough to irritate you: exactness has an altitude.

The next caption calls the accounts “fragmentary but invaluable,” which is the first phrase in the wing you would not amend. One message contradicts the driver’s timing. Another was copied decades after the event from a damaged original. A route tally has been added wrong by one. Their limitations are printed below them in calm museum language. The small records are allowed uncertainty. Only the queen has been polished until nothing partial remains.

At the end of the case, a final panel asks whether Sol-*steece* Evening Bell was truly alone.

The text offers the Twelve as an answer. It calls them possible ghosts, symbolic companions, or later inventions meant to soften the terrible solitude of heroism.

You were the only living combatant over the Bay. That matters. No other person could take a position beside you, warn you of a needle flight, catch you when a bell-step ended in sleet. The twelve could not speak or choose. Calling them companions would invent life where none was stored.

Calling you unaided would erase their choices.

And below, beyond your attention, drivers carried civilians east. Dispatchers emptied roads. Weather observers kept instruments running under a sky they could barely read. They did not fight the host. They made it possible for a battle over an evacuated shore to remain one.

On the plaque, *alone* has to cover the sky, the crown, and every road below. It cannot.

You read the source note. Then the image credit. Then the donor acknowledgment for the case. Your promise was every caption, and museums hide their most revealing claims in small print.

The remaining wall takes forty-three minutes.

You learn which governments have lent facsimiles, which alloys were guessed for the unrecovered frames, which poet first placed a sword in your hand, and how many schoolchildren voted for the reconstructed crown’s color. You read a sanitation notice on the touch table. You read the label beneath a bench explaining that its wood came from storm-felled trees planted long after the battle.

Closing tones begin while you are bent over the fire-capacity plate beside the exit. You straighten too quickly and cross two floor triggers. The audio bead overlays a solemn account of your “final sword form” with instructions to return the device at reception. For several seconds your mythical weapon is available in six languages and must not be placed in a pocket or waste bin.

You laugh. It surprises you enough that the two tracks end before you move again.

The testimony alcove stands beyond the exhibition proper, a padded recess with one stool and a recording lens. A sign invites family stories, inherited traditions, and first-hand witness accounts. You nearly pass it. The categories have the soft, posthumous air of everything in the wing. They are built for grandchildren carrying a box of letters, not for the grammatical subject of the plaques.

The screen brightens as you approach.

**TELL US YOUR CONNECTION TO THE BATTLE OF THE BAY.**

You sit.

The form asks for your life story first. It offers prompts about childhood, coronation, grief, and the burden of survival. You skip them. It asks whether you possess an artifact for scanning. You select no. It asks what proof of identity you can provide.

You leave the field empty.

The recording lens opens. In its small black surface, you look less like the glass silhouette than the tired visitor you are: plain coat, museum bead, hair flattened on one side where the clip has pressed for hours. You could authenticate yourself in a dozen spectacular ways, none of which would prove a count. A bright seam through the wall would establish only that you could make one.

You press record.

“My name is Solstice Evening Bell.” You say it slowly, correctly, without giving the machine a performance to admire. “I am the person your exhibition calls the First Monarch. I was present above the Bay. I am recording four corrections limited to what I witnessed and what I carried.”

The red mark beside the lens holds steady.

“The host consisted of 131,072 nonliving autonomous frames: eight wedges of 16,384. I counted them through royal hearing. I did not carry a sword. The crown did not contain twelve spirits, minds, or persons. It contained twelve final spells, freely made by twelve adults whose souls and minds had passed on. Those works required my living agency, and all twelve were destroyed during the battle.

“I was the only living combatant above the Bay. I was not unaided. I cannot testify to the evacuation as it was experienced from the shore, and I do not authorize the museum to treat my account as a complete history of the event.”

You stop there.

The form asks if you would like to add the donors’ names. No. It asks permission to extract clips for promotional use. No. To preserve the raw recording for research and accession review: yes. To quote the four corrections, unaltered and with the limits you stated: yes. To synthesize or revoice your speech: no.

Relationship to the subject offers seven choices. Descendant. Family. Scholar. Community custodian. Eyewitness. Other.

At the bottom, perhaps included for people recording about themselves in more ordinary exhibitions, is **SELF**.

You select it.

The automatic transcript appears. It has spelled the number correctly. It has turned *Bell* into *Belle* and supplied *Sol-steece* as a pronunciation note beside your name.

An edit button waits.

You leave the text attached to the raw voice. The accession status reads **UNVERIFIED — PENDING REVIEW**. You submit before the screen can offer another prompt.

At reception, you return the audio bead. As you cross the outer hall, another visitor steps into the painted lane behind you.

“Sol-*steece* Evening Bell,” the guide begins, “stood alone against countless invaders—”

You continue through the doors before it reaches the sword.

stories.title: The Wolf in the Mirror
stories.prompt: You were fully prepared to watch over your cursed partner while they transform into werewolf on the full moon. What you were not prepared for was them chasing their tail for 2 hours and then barking at themselves after walking in front of mirror.
stories.body:
# The Wolf in the Mirror

The bite-resistant coat was for getting Teague off me without losing an arm. The plywood panel was for dividing the room if they became territorial. The canvas straps were for restraint, but only if the alternative was a broken window, an open door, or a throat.

The spray bottle was water. The air horn was noise. The first-aid kit was obvious.

At eight forty-three, with moonrise twenty-six minutes away, I sat cross-legged on the padded floor of our spare room and assigned every object its catastrophe.

Teague leaned in the doorway, holding two mugs of tea. “What’s the towel for?”

I looked down at the folded towel beside the emergency kit. It had somehow escaped my list.

“Blood,” I said.

“Charming.” They passed me a mug. “Could it be for tea instead?”

“If we spill tea, we’ll have a towel.”

“There. You’re adapting already.”

They were trying to make the room look less like a place we had built in case love failed under pressure. It did not work. We had taken the bed apart and stacked the frame and mattress in the hall. I had covered the baseboards with foam pipe insulation, screwed a temporary brace across the window, and laid interlocking gym mats wall to wall. The mirrored closet doors wore an old gray sheet, fastened at the top with six black clamps. Everything scented had gone: soap, laundry powder, the cedar blocks Teague kept in their sweaters. I had cleaned with hot water and the unscented liquid we used for the dishes.

The room smelled of rubber mats, weak tea, and the plastic backing of medical tape.

Teague stepped inside and shut the door. “Last check.”

We had done the check twice. I put down my mug.

They pointed to the straps. “Only if I’m going to get out or seriously hurt one of us.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t put yourself between me and the door.”

“I use the panel.”

“And if the panel doesn’t work?”

“I leave, lock the door behind me, and call the number on the fridge.”

“You don’t come back in because I sound upset.”

That was the part they always watched my face for.

“I don’t come back in.”

They nodded. Their tea trembled once against the rim of the mug. “The bruises last month were mostly on my shoulders. Scratches on my legs. Nothing that looked like a bite.”

“You told me.”

“I know. I’m telling myself.” They set the mug outside in the hall. “I remember the change. After that, pieces. A smell like wet concrete. Waking up under the workbench. I don’t know what I did in between.”

The last three full moons, Teague had locked themself in the detached garage of the house we rented. They had refused to let me watch until the bruises became too numerous to dismiss and one fingernail came back split to the quick. This month, they had drawn the room plan. They had chosen the barriers, approved the straps, and made me rehearse the lock.

Now they held out their hand. “Still willing?”

It was not a question about courage. It was permission renewed while they could give it, and an offer to stop.

I took their hand. “Yes.”

“Stay where I can see you, then.”

At nine-oh-six, I locked the door.

The change began before I had returned the key to the zippered pocket inside my coat.

Teague made one startled sound and dropped to a knee. I reached for them, remembered the plan, and stopped with my hand in the air. Heat rolled off their skin. Their fingers spread against the mat as the nails darkened and thickened. Their shoulders drew high; their shirt split at one seam, then vanished beneath a rush of coarse brown-black fur.

No part of it was neat. Their body worked furiously against a shape it had known all day. Bones shifted under skin. Breath became panting, panting became a growl too low for the room, and the room seemed to shrink around it.

I had prepared for teeth. I had not understood the size of the animal that would carry them.

When it was over, a wolf stood where Teague had knelt, taller at the shoulder than the plywood panel was wide. Their paws pressed divots into the gym mats. Their claws clicked once when they adjusted their weight. One amber eye caught the ceiling light; the other remained in shadow.

The coat suddenly felt decorative.

“Teague,” I said.

Their ears turned toward me.

Then their head swung back toward their hindquarters.

I took hold of the panel. A feint, I thought. Predators watched one direction and moved in another. I had read that somewhere in the frantic, useless week when every search for *first time supervising cursed partner* had given me either folklore or advertisements.

Teague’s tail flicked.

Their eyes fixed on it.

The tail flicked again.

Teague pounced.

They missed by the length of their muzzle. The tail escaped to the left. Teague wheeled after it, hind paws skidding on the mats, and completed one astonished circle.

They stopped. The tail swayed behind them.

I lowered the panel by an inch.

Teague turned their head slowly. The tail moved out of reach.

They lunged after it again.

By the fifth circle, I understood what I was seeing. By the tenth, I accepted that understanding it did not tell me how to stop it.

“Teague.”

Their ears twitched as they passed me, but their feet did not slow.

“Enough.”

That was our stop word. Human Teague had chosen it because, in their opinion, panic made subtle vocabulary irresponsible. Wolf Teague showed no respect for its design.

I set the padded panel in their path.

They dodged it. This was encouraging for half a second. Then the dodge carried them into a tighter turn around me, and they accelerated as if I had introduced rules to a game.

I raised the panel and backed toward the wall. “No. Not a course. This is not a course.”

Teague’s tongue appeared at one side of their mouth. Their forepaws drummed the floor. Each lap brought the thick sweep of their shoulder closer to my knees.

I retreated behind the equipment pile and began moving everything out of the circle.

The straps went onto the windowsill. The first-aid kit followed. I was shifting the emergency water when Teague cut too close and clipped the spray bottle with one rear paw. It spun across the floor. They chased that for three strides, decided it was beneath consideration, and rediscovered the tail with renewed delight.

At nine-fourteen, I opened the incident log.

*Transformation complete approximately 21:11,* I wrote. *Subject began continuous clockwise circling at approximately 21:14. Appears focused on own tail.*

I stared at the sentence. Filling in the log kept my hands from interfering, so I added: *Has not caught it.*

At nine-twenty, Teague’s orbit widened enough to graze the wall. Their tail struck the foam-covered baseboard with a soft, regular thump. I wedged the towel into the corner where their hind paw kept slipping. Blood had not touched it. Neither had tea.

At nine-twenty-seven, I tried water. I slid the metal bowl into the outer edge of their path when they seemed to be slowing.

Teague stepped in it.

Water sheeted across the mats. The bowl shot under the closet door. Teague stopped so abruptly that their back legs folded. For one hopeful moment, they sat in the puddle and panted at me.

“Good,” I whispered. “Stay.”

Their tail flopped against the wet floor.

Their head snapped around.

“Don’t.”

The chase resumed counterclockwise.

I updated the log.

At nine-thirty-nine, their nose passed near the open emergency kit. Teague recoiled as if struck. Their muzzle wrinkled; their whole body gathered around one tremendous sneeze that slammed their chin into the mat.

They stared at the kit. So did I.

Inside the top compartment, under the gauze and tape, was a foil packet of citrus cleaning wipes I had bought months ago and forgotten.

“Sorry.”

Teague sneezed again. I bagged the packet, zipped it inside a second bag, and sealed both inside the lidded waste bucket. While my back was turned, Teague found their tail again.

By ten o’clock, the room had been reorganized around the chase. Every hard object except the water bowl was outside the orbit or flat against a wall. I had looped the straps through the window brace so no paw could tangle in them, used the blood towel to pad the skid corner, and refilled the bowl with less than an inch so Teague could drink in the rare pauses without flooding the floor.

They drank twice. Both times, their tail moved before they had finished. Both times, they abandoned the bowl mid-lap and sprayed water from their muzzle across my trousers.

I did not laugh.

This felt important at the time.

Teague feared the curse. They feared what happened in the missing hours and what I might see there. They had trusted me to guard them, not to gather a private supply of amusing stories. So I kept my mouth set and my pen busy while an enormous werewolf spun past me with a look of radiant determination.

At ten-seventeen, the chase slowed from a gallop to a determined trot. At ten-thirty-six, Teague lay down, captured the tip of their tail between both front paws, and tried to bite it. The tail escaped. They sprang up with a grunt and began again.

At ten-fifty-two, I noticed that the upper-left clamp on the closet sheet had shaken loose. The sheet sagged enough to show a thumb-wide strip of mirror. Reaching it meant crossing the circle. I decided a sliver of glass was safer than a collision and wrote *replace clamp when movement stops* in the log.

At eleven-oh-five, concern finally did what fear had failed to do and made me sensible. Teague was panting hard. Their steps dragged at the end of each turn, and the pads of their paws had begun to squeak on the rubber. I wanted to stop them. Every method I had prepared depended on aggression or escape: block, startle, restrain, withdraw. None accounted for a partner who was hurting themself with enthusiasm.

I put away the air horn. I took off the heavy forearm guards because their buckles could catch fur if Teague fell against me. Then I sat outside the circle with the water bowl between my boots and waited for the tail to lose its argument.

At eleven-fourteen, exactly two hours after the first complete turn, Teague stopped.

Momentum carried their hindquarters another quarter circle. Their front paws attempted a correction, crossed, and folded. They landed on their chest with a floor-shaking *whump*.

I was up before I remembered not to rush them.

“Teague?”

They stood on the second try. Their legs were sound, though they placed each paw as if the floor had developed opinions. They drank the whole shallow bowl. Then they wandered toward the closet, swaying gently.

The loose clamp fell.

The sheet peeled from the mirror in a slow diagonal, exposing a second exhausted wolf and a pale person in an oversized protective coat.

Teague froze.

The reflected wolf froze.

Their ears rose. The other wolf’s ears rose too.

Teague barked.

The sound hit the walls hard enough to sting my face. The wolf in the mirror barked back without delay.

Teague jumped sideways, struck the dented water bowl, and barked again. Their reflection performed the same assault. Teague lowered their head and showed their teeth. The other wolf knew that trick.

“Teague.”

No response.

“Enough.”

They barked over me.

“Back.”

They advanced on the glass. I snatched up the panel, but when its edge appeared in the mirror, Teague wheeled toward it with a growl. I let it drop. The impact made them whip back to the rival.

Every answer made the question louder. Bark, recoil, bark. Claws scraped the mats as Teague charged and checked themself short of the glass. The mirror held, but the closet doors shuddered in their frame.

I looked for the angle that would let me reach the fallen sheet. Instead I saw what Teague saw: two wolves squared in a bare padded room, with two ridiculous wardens behind them. My coat reached nearly to my shins. One sleeve was soaked. A strip of silver tape clung to my hip. My hair stood upright where the helmet had pressed it, and I was holding an empty spray bottle like a ceremonial weapon.

Two hours of swallowed laughter escaped at once.

It was not graceful laughter. It started as a snort, broke in the middle, and became the helpless wheeze Teague claimed sounded like a screen door losing a fight.

The barking stopped.

Teague turned from the mirror.

Their ears eased sideways. Their mouth remained open, showing every tooth I had spent a week imagining, but the growl was gone. They looked at me for three panting seconds. Then their tail struck the floor once.

Still laughing, quieter now, I moved sideways along the wall. I kept myself out of the space between Teague and the glass. Their eyes followed me. When I reached the fallen corner of the sheet, I crouched, caught it, and drew it across the mirror from the side.

The rival wolf vanished.

Teague inspected the cloth. They sniffed the place where the other animal had been, sneezed once in what I chose not to take personally, and leaned their shoulder against my boot.

Their weight nearly tipped me over.

I sat. After a moment, Teague lowered themself beside me with a groan. I unzipped the coat so they would not rest against the hard fasteners. They put their muzzle across my ankle, hot and heavy, and closed their eyes.

I stayed awake until dawn, watching the sheet.

The return was no kinder than the change. When Teague’s paws became hands again, I covered them with the coat and waited until they could speak before I touched them. Their first word was water. Their second was my name. Their third was “Damage?”

“You’re sore. Your paws were intact before the change back. There’s a scrape on one knee now.” I helped them sit against the wall and handed over the bottle. “No bites. No broken glass. No escape attempt.”

They drank, winced, and examined me over the rim. “You?”

“Bruised dignity.”

“From me?”

“Mostly the coat.”

We waited until they could stand before leaving the room. I made toast while Teague showered and dressed. By breakfast, they had the incident log beside their plate and the suspicious expression they used when instructions omitted a step.

“You skipped from transformation complete to no one got hurt.”

I buttered the same corner of my toast for too long.

“I gave you the important part.”

“You gave me the medical part.” Teague tapped the log. “What happened for the rest of it?”

I had considered editing the account. Not lying; only choosing the details that preserved the gravity of the night. But Teague had not asked me to preserve their gravity. They had asked me to watch.

“You chased your tail,” I said.

They waited.

“For two hours.”

“Two hours?”

“I rearranged the whole room. You reversed direction once. There was a citrus-wipe incident.”

Teague covered their eyes with one hand.

“Then the mirror covering fell.”

Their hand lowered. “Oh no.”

“You barked at yourself.”

“Once?”

“It became a disagreement.”

They looked toward the hall, where the spare-room door remained locked. Embarrassment warmed their face, but they did not look away from me. “How did you stop it?”

“I laughed.”

Teague absorbed that. “And?”

“You looked at me. I covered the mirror. You lay down.”

They pulled the log closer and read every entry, including *Has not caught it.* I did not apologize for that line. They did not ask me to.

“Next month,” they said at last, “we keep the barrier.”

“Definitely.”

“Two water bowls. Heavy ones.”

“Agreed.”

“Clear the whole middle before we start. Better clamps on the sheet. And you’re allowed to laugh if I’m not injured or trying to eat you.”

“That is a difficult standard to assess in real time.”

“Put it in the plan.”

I took the pen. Teague reached across the table and stopped my hand before I could write.

“Wait,” they said. “Did I ever catch it?”

“No.”

Their relief arrived first. The laughter followed, hoarse from barking and careful of their aching side, but entirely their own.

stories.title: Thirteen Years Borrowed
stories.prompt: You can posses people for a day. For the past thirteen years, you have been looking for your original body.
stories.body:
# Thirteen Years Borrowed

The tooth is mine.

I know before I have finished taking the body. The right incisor catches the
inside of the lower lip, a tiny hooked edge where I chipped it on an apricot
stone at sixteen. Then the rest of the body closes around me: sight, weight,
the drag of a canvas bag on one shoulder, the cold brass knob beneath my hand.
I settle into the bones as into a house seen after a fire and rebuilt without
the plans.

The left fourth toe aches in the rain. I broke it kicking a bed frame and lied
about the limp for a week. The right arm reaches farther than I expect because
I have spent thirteen years measuring reach in other people's proportions.
The jaw is heavier. The lungs are shallower. The heart bangs hard enough to
blur the dim hallway.

Mine, every beat says. Mine, mine, mine.

*Get out,* says a woman inside my attention.

I let the hand fall from the apartment door. Beyond the stairwell window,
morning is a gray strip between buildings. The watch on the wrist reads 6:17.

*Now.*

My relief has nowhere to go. It shakes the knees instead. I lean against the
wall and press my tongue to the broken tooth again, as if certainty needs a
second witness.

"My name is Eamon Huxley," I say with a voice deeper than the one I remember.
"This is my body."

The woman goes quiet for three heartbeats. I feel none of her thoughts, only
the silence where her chosen words would be. A person possessed stays awake.
They feel everything I make their body do and remember the whole day, but I
cannot rummage through memory. It was the first mercy I found in the thing
that happened to me, and later the most useful excuse.

*My name is Nadira Whitlock,* she says. *You have stolen my hands in my own hallway.
Get out of me.*

I have left people after seconds when a scar was wrong, a knuckle too broad,
an old fracture absent. I have also stayed when doubt required more looking.
Whatever body I enter throws me out after twenty-four hours. Between bodies I
am almost nothing: direction, pressure, the faint wash of nearby voices. I
cannot see my way across a room. For thirteen years, the day has been a prison
and a promise.

"I need to know if it keeps me."

*You know the tooth. Congratulations. Leave.*

"The toe too. And the shoulder blade has a flat place on the left. There'll be
a white scar under the ribs, curved like a comma."

The body's mouth closes under my control. Nadira cannot stop it. By the time she
answers, I have clenched the jaw hard enough to make it ache.

*There is,* she says. *I still want my hands.*

"At 6:17 tomorrow, maybe the choice won't be mine."

*And until then?*

I look down at the unfamiliar coat, the ink stain on one cuff, the keys looped
around two fingers. The left wrist wears a black brace. These things feel like
evidence I have not yet sorted.

"Until then, I stay."

Inside the apartment, Nadira makes me remove my shoes before she will say another
word. I nearly laugh. She feels it in the chest and tells me not to.

The rooms are small and exact. A plant turns broad leaves toward the kitchen
window. Awls and brushes stand in jars on a worktable against one wall, though
Nadira informs me that the real bench is downstairs. Three pairs of reading
glasses wait where different tasks require them. The body knows none of this
for me. My hand reaches toward the wrong drawer for a spoon, and only Nadira's
sharp *left* keeps me from opening a box of powdered pigments.

In the bathroom I find the scar under the ribs. I lift the pajama shirt beneath
the day clothes and stare at its pale curve in the mirror. A pan handle did
that when I was eleven. I find the mole behind the right knee and the shallow
dent at the crown of the skull. Each recognition loosens something that has
been clenched in me for years.

But there are additions. A silver line crosses the base of the thumb. The
fingertips are rough in patterns I never earned. A tendon shifts painfully
beneath the wrist brace. There are two small holes in one earlobe, a missing
molar, faint creases bracketing the mouth. I put on the glasses Nadira directs me
to, and the labels on the medicine cabinet snap into focus.

*You are holding my neck at a ridiculous angle,* she says.

I straighten. The right shoulder still complains.

"What happened to it?"

*A press slipped last winter. I caught the platen because the alternative was
letting it crush a nineteenth-century prayer book.*

"You saved a book with my shoulder?"

*I injured my shoulder at work.*

The mirror gives us one face and no way to divide the expression. I stop
looking.

Nadira has porridge in the refrigerator and insists the body needs food before
coffee. I taste the jam before spooning it into the bowl. Sourness bites the
sides of my tongue.

*That jar is sweet,* she says.

"Not while I'm here. Sweet and sour trade places."

*That's absurd.*

"It's consistent."

*You prefer absurdity with records.*

I open the refrigerator and take out a jar of pickled onions to prove it. The
brine coats my mouth like warm syrup. Nadira tastes the same mouthful normally
and swears so vividly that I choke.

"I usually eat plain food."

*You usually do this?*

The question waits while I rinse the onion taste away. "I usually have to eat."

Nadira directs me to oats, salt, and a banana. My hand reaches automatically for
the sugar bowl, not from her habit but mine, then stops. I cannot trust the
tongue to season for the person feeling it with me. We eat the porridge plain.

At the table she asks where I was thirteen years ago.

There have been so many versions of this account, spoken to frightened
strangers and skeptical healers and one old man who tried to sell me a glass
body. In this mouth the facts feel indecently simple.

"A public washroom near the bus depot. I was washing ink off my fingers. I
blinked and I was outside, in a man waiting by the ticket machines. He started
screaming in my head. When the day ended, I fell into a woman on a bench. Then
someone on a bus. I couldn't get back inside the washroom without taking
someone who was going there. By the time I managed it, this body was gone."

Nadira does not answer at once. The refrigerator hums; rain ticks against the
window. When she answers, each clause is neat and bloodless, as if she has
pared away anything I might mistake for a plea.

*My first memory is sitting on the floor of a public washroom,* she says. *My
hands were wet. There was ink in the sink. I knew how to speak and read. I knew
what buses were and that I should not be barefoot in a public building. I did
not know my name, where I lived, or why the face in the mirror made me expect
someone else.*

The body's fingers have curled around the bowl. I make them release it.

"The date?"

She gives it. The same date. I ask the time, but she never found out. I ask
whether she saw anyone leave, whether there was a sound, a light, a smell of
ozone, a missing hour. Her answers shorten until they become one answer.

*I don't know.*

I have spent thirteen years believing that enough physical detail would lead
to an explanation. Here is the body, every private mark intact, and the cause
is no closer than when I was blind beside the ticket machines.

"Why did you leave?"

*Because a custodian was knocking. Because there were identification cards in
the wallet with a name I did not recognize, and the address had been emptied.
Because after three days of asking people to tell me who I was, I understood
that none of them could.*

"So you chose Nadira Whitlock."

*Eventually. I chose breakfast first.*

Dry laughter moves through the body before I decide whether to permit it. It is
hers in timing and mine in muscle, and the distinction troubles me more than
the scar did.

At eight, Nadira tells me we have to go downstairs.

"No."

*I promised a repair by noon.*

"Tell them you're ill."

*You have my voice, not my judgment. I prepared everything yesterday. The
collector only needs to find the package in the front cabinet.*

"Then it can sit there unfinished."

*If you intend to occupy my body all day, you can at least refrain from
damaging my business while you do it.*

I want to bolt the door, strip, and map every old hurt against my memory. I
want to walk until the gait becomes mine again. Instead I follow her directions
to a narrow workroom on the ground floor, because hiding in her apartment
would require ignoring the life around the body, and I have become less able
to do that than I was an hour ago.

The room smells of paste, leather, and damp paper. A press squats beside the
bench. Shelves hold books in stages of undress: boards removed, spines exposed,
pages lifted into careful fans. On the bench lies a school atlas with its cover
off. A torn map at the front has been flattened beneath glass. Along one margin,
a child's pencil has added a sea monster with six worried eyes.

*Wash your hands. Cold water. Dry them on the linen, not the blue rag.*

"I know how to wash hands."

*Those hands? So far I have seen no evidence.*

I obey. Nadira talks me through removing the glass and lifting the mended page.
The sheet is so thin it flutters when I breathe. Beside it waits a strip of
toned paper, nearly invisible against the torn margin.

"I remember being good with my hands," I tell her.

*You may have been. Pick up the folder.*

I choose the flat steel tool.

*The bone folder.*

"That is bone?"

*It has been a common tool longer than either of us has used these fingers.
The cream-colored one.*

I set the wrong tool down. The folder fits the palm with intimate unfamiliarity.
Nadira tells me to test the grain of the repair paper. I bend it one way, then the
other, feeling no difference.

*Again. Smaller bend.*

"It feels the same."

*It is not.*

I reach for the knife.

*Stop.*

The word strikes so hard I freeze with the blade above the paper.

*If you cut across the grain, it will pull the page when the humidity changes.
Put it down.*

"You said the collector comes at noon."

*Then we have time to do it slowly.*

The hands are mine by bone length, Nadira's by every useful callus, and presently
good at nothing. I put down the knife.

We begin again. She has me lift an edge, bend it, listen as well as feel. Across
the grain the paper gives a faint dry resistance. Along it, the curve comes
easily. Once I catch the difference, I cannot understand how I missed it.

That thought is dangerous. I cut too confidently, and the wrist twinges beneath
the brace.

*Rest the heel of the hand,* Nadira says. Her anger has changed shape. *Let the
knife travel. Do not make the wrist pull it.*

I adjust. The blade whispers through the strip.

The work takes the morning. Nadira gives instructions in distances smaller than I
can see without the strongest glasses. I mix paste too thin, then nearly ruin
the second batch by tasting a dab and reaching for salt.

*Paste is not soup.*

"It tastes sweet."

*It tastes sour because it has spoiled. Throw it away.*

We start a third batch. I learn the brush is rolled, not dragged, and that a
page can be damp enough to relax without looking wet. When the shoulder burns,
Nadira has me lower the stool. When my impatience makes the brush jump, she stops
speaking. After twelve quiet seconds, I set it down.

By eleven thirty, the repaired map lies flat. The join is visible only when I
tilt it toward the lamp. I paste new cloth to the spine, fit the cover, and set
the atlas between boards in the small press. We turn the screw together only
