He was protecting grain carts, wages, and judgments by forcing my sibling into the chair without the truth.

The captain read to the end of the clause. Then he signaled the door guards.

The bars rose. The potter entered first, still carrying the pipe; the prophet followed. Clerks, petitioners, guards, and the master of works crowded onto the public floor, far more than twelve.

Father watched my sibling approach the rail.

“You found the black book,” he said.

“You left it where the minister could hide it.”

“Yes.” Father's gaze dropped to the commission in my hand, and his mouth tightened. “I knew the prophet's wording because I had read the old formula last month. I was not afraid of a knife from either of you. I did not know which lawful choice you would make.”

“You knew we had choices we didn't know about.”

“I meant to tell you after I had answers for the council's objections.”

“The bell answered first,” I said.

Father looked at the iron cradle, the locked doors now lifting, the clerk's shortened transcript. His calm had gone. “Put the bell in the charges.”

The first minister raised the incapacity sheet. “At moonrise this proceeding will transfer the office without risking an obsolete break in authority. There are twenty-five minutes. Continue it, and every current obligation remains legible.”

My sibling looked past him at the throne. They had practiced sitting there for ceremonies since childhood. I had never seen them touch it except when ordered.

They stepped to the witness rail.

“Before this open hall, I call for the death of the crown.”

The clerk's pen stopped. The captain opened the bronze drawer beneath the right arm of the throne. Inside its frame lay Father's reign-seal: black wax as wide as my palm, bearing the signet mark at its center. It had hardened for twenty-three years.

My sibling did not look at me again.

“First charge,” they said. “The king kept the three-bell order after learning that his own command could not stop it. Today it imprisoned his children on an untested accusation and made his care for them legally irrelevant.”

The captain testified to the order. I placed the clerk's shortened prophecy beside its wet-sanded gap. The prophet repeated the missing words once, flat and exact.

Father gripped the protection rail. “I kept the order after the gate attack because guards needed an instruction faster than panic. I marked the appeal for amendment and did not finish it. The charge is true.”

“Second charge. The succession oath binds the first heir to an office they formally refused. The king knew the refusal had no docket. He let the law remain while the council prepared to use it.”

My sibling's rejected petition went onto the rail, its green cord bright against the wood. The registrar who had brought documents to the council recognized his own seal and confirmed the rejection.

Father answered more slowly. “I could not open the office without protecting the warrants attached to it. I chose to settle the accounts first.”

“You chose the order of danger,” my sibling said. “We carried the part you postponed.”

Father looked toward the public benches. The potter's pipe dripped onto the floor between his shoes. “The charge is true.”

My sibling laid Father's memorandum over the old register.

“Third charge. He prepared a remedy in secret. He did not tell either child about crown-death, the planned assembly, or the law that would seize us if his work ran late. He trusted his intention more than our need to know.”

“I kept it from the council until the contracts were safe,” Father said.

“You kept it from us as well.”

“I did not trust this room with it.”

“You made us live inside this room's power.”

Father turned toward the throne. No one spoke for him.

He touched the place on his finger where the signet usually rested. “The charge is true.”

The first minister checked the eastern windows. A pale edge of moonlight had reached the highest pane. “The sovereign may contest the remedy. Nothing requires him to yield.”

“Nothing does,” Father said.

He held out his hand to the captain. The iron cradle was unlocked by two council keys. The captain placed the signet in Father's palm.

Father weighed it, then offered it across the rail to my sibling. “I yield the sovereign office. If you accept it, break the seal.”

My sibling took the ring. Their hand shook badly enough that the heavy gold clicked against the bronze frame. They stopped, set their feet, and looked once at the public doors, once at the commission I held, and once at Father.

Then they brought the signet's face down.

The black disk split through its old impression. One half jumped from the frame and struck the floor. The clerk dipped his pen and entered the time in the register.

“The king is dead,” the captain said.

Father remained standing before us, bareheaded and breathing. When he moved toward the dais, the captain lowered an arm across his path. The yielded king could not approach the chair until the next sovereign permitted it.

Father stopped. The hurt on his face was small and unguarded. Then he stepped back to the public side of the rail.

My sibling climbed the three steps and sat.

The first minister brought them the unfinished incapacity order. “The seals for tonight's grain warrants must be recut. The garrison pay chests require a living signature before midnight. The council will need a ruling on every contract naming the former sovereign.”

No one had given my sibling a circlet. They looked more trapped without one.

“Preserve every record from today,” they said. “Unlock the rooms closed by the three-bell order. No detention continues without an accusation a clerk will sign. The warrants come here. The rest of the succession law waits for an open assembly, and I will not promise when that work ends.”

The minister began to object to the order of tasks.

“Bring the grain warrants first,” my sibling said. “You numbered the risk. We will use your list.”

He looked at the throne, recalculated, and bowed.

The moon cleared the eastern roofs. Its light reached the broken reign-seal and the wet length of pipe lying beside it.

The potter was still waiting.

My sibling pointed to the witness rail. “Set the pipe there. Tell me where the water turns.”

Father took a place on the public bench. I pulled the unused clerk's chair to the right of the throne, put the green commission beneath my coat, and opened a fresh page while the potter began.

stories.title: What the Town Owed Her
stories.prompt: The gothic witch that lives in apartment next to you looks incredible youthful but it seems like every family in town owes her something.
stories.body:
# What the Town Owed Her

By the time I unlocked my grandmother's apartment, three families had visited the witch next door.

I knew they were three families, though only five people climbed the stairs. Mirehaven had a way of making ancestry visible. You could tell which children belonged to the woman from the bakery by the flour worked into the seams of their coats, and which old man had married into the hardware family because he carried a paper parcel tied with their particular blue string. They came separately through the rain, knocked at number six, and offered up a jar of honey, a coil of copper wire, and a key without a lock.

The woman who accepted them looked no older than twenty-five.

She wore a black dress buttoned to the throat and cuffs narrow enough to make her hands seem delicate. Her hair was the brown-black of wet bark, pinned in a style I knew from the photographs in my grandmother's sitting room. Not similar to it. The same.

The old man saw me watching and lowered his voice.

“My grandfather said she'd ask when the town needed us.”

“Not today,” the young woman told him. She returned the key to his palm and folded his fingers over it. “Keep it where you can find it quickly.”

He obeyed with the relief of a man who had been refused a sentence.

Then she turned to me. Her face was lovely in the severe, improbable way of a saint carved into a tomb.

“You are the Sayer granddaughter.”

“Leonie.”

“Evadne Trell.”

Behind her, number six was lit by candles despite the gray afternoon. Bundles of drying plants hung from a brass rail. Their shadows stirred when no draft touched my face.

“My grandmother said you were a witch,” I told her.

“Your grandmother said many accurate things in an unhelpful tone.” Evadne glanced at the keys in my hand. “You should check the cellar before you sign anything.”

I had come to empty number five, sell it, and leave before Mirehaven remembered enough about me to start making demands. The buyers were due in two days. Their surveyor had already found damp in the basement, but old buildings had damp, and Rookglass House was older than most excuses. Its stone angels had lost their faces to salt. Its gutters spilled brown ropes of water down the windows. Nothing about it had ever been dry, level, or easy to heat.

Inside, my grandmother's rooms waited in perfect order. Her slippers stood under the bed. A cup with a faint crescent of lipstick rested beside the sink, as if death had interrupted her between sips and she meant to complain about the intrusion when she returned.

I began with the desk because grief could not hide inside a bank statement. Three hours later I had made piles for the solicitor, the charity shop, and the bin. The rain thickened against the glass. Water gurgled somewhere in the walls.

At the back of the lowest drawer lay an envelope with my name on it.

Inside was one line in my grandmother's square hand.

*When Evadne asks, open the east cellar wall.*

I read it twice, then carried it next door.

Evadne opened before I knocked. The honey, copper wire, and key were not in sight.

“What is in the wall?” I asked.

“Something your grandmother believed should remain closed until it was needed.”

“And when will that be?”

She listened. At first I thought the pose theatrical. Then I heard a low vibration beneath the building, too steady for thunder.

“Possibly tonight.”

I laughed. She did not.

My telephone rang inside number five. The estate agent had photographs from the surveyor: a wet fracture had appeared along the basement's eastern side. Until its cause was known, the buyers would not exchange contracts.

“There goes possibly,” Evadne said.

I shut my door in her face.

At eleven, hammering woke me on the sofa. I had fallen asleep among boxes with my grandmother's note clenched in one hand. The electric lights flickered. Something struck stone below, paused, then struck twice more.

The cellar stairs smelled of wet iron. My torch found Evadne kneeling beside the east wall, measuring a crack with a dressmaker's rule. She had changed into boots and a man's old wool coat, though the black skirt still brushed her ankles. Water shone between the floor tiles.

“You asked me to open this,” I said.

“I haven't asked yet.”

“You sent three generations of dead people to do it for you.”

On a stool behind her lay a thick book bound in scuffed green leather. Beside it sat a tin of photographs. I recognized Evadne in the top one, standing in ankle-deep floodwater among women in long aprons and men with watch chains. On the back, a date had been written more than a century ago.

The next photograph showed her outside Rookglass House when its stone angels still had faces. In the next, she held a child in a coat from the years of my grandmother's youth. Her dress changed. Her expression did not. So little as a line had appeared around her eyes.

I opened the book.

The entries began in several different hands, then settled into Evadne's narrow script. A family rescued when the old river flooded its banks: *anything in our power, whenever you name it.* A baby delivered while fire trapped the midwife across town: *anything.* Two brothers found alive in winter scrub: *we will answer you, whenever.* A widow sheltered from a violent husband. A roof held through a storm. Medicine brought through snow.

The last column on every page was marked *unanswered*.

“They tell children they owe you,” I said. “They bring offerings. They lower their voices when they say your name.”

“Yes.”

“And you stand there looking younger than their grandchildren.”

“Also yes.”

Anger felt cleaner than the fear moving under my ribs. “What do you take from them?”

Evadne rose. “Nothing they don't give.”

“Their years?”

For the first time, her composure broke. Not much; a tightening at one corner of her mouth. “Do you think I would choose to watch a century pass through this town one funeral at a time?”

She turned the ledger toward herself. Her finger rested on the first page, where rain had feathered the oldest ink.

“When the first flood came, I kept a dozen people alive in the upper rooms of this building until the water fell. I was young, frightened, and far too pleased with my own power. They promised me anything. I let the promise stand.” She looked toward the wall. “Whatever answers vows in Mirehaven fixed me at the age I was when that first one went unanswered. Each open promise added another knot. I cannot grow older, and I cannot cross the town boundary.”

“Convenient punishment.”

“There are worse faces to be trapped inside.” Her voice went flat. “That does not make it freedom.”

“Then ask for a loaf of bread from each of them. Cross out the lines. Walk away.”

“The people who spoke those promises are dead. Their descendants did not consent to them.”

“You let the descendants think they did.”

This time she had no quick answer.

Rain rattled the pavement grates outside. The vibration under our feet deepened.

“I told each household they could refuse,” she said. “I accepted gifts when refusing them would have been cruel, but I did not call the gifts payment. And I waited because the old relief channel would be needed again. When it is opened, it takes half the town to clear it and one witch to keep the roof from falling. I thought the promises might make them listen long enough to choose.”

“You kept them afraid because one day fear might be useful.”

“Yes.” She met my eyes. “I have had time to become wrong in several directions.”

The wall gave a soft crack. A thread of black water pushed through the mortar and ran over the toe of her boot.

I went upstairs to find proof.

My grandmother had kept Rookglass House's repair bills in a kitchen cupboard, sorted by year and tied with string. Behind them lay a cardboard tube containing plans drawn on waxed linen. The oldest showed a stone channel branching from the river, passing beneath the building, and rejoining the marsh below the lower streets. A red line marked a manual spillway behind the east cellar wall.

Later sheets carried my grandmother's measurements. The main culvert had bowed inward. If it collapsed during a surge, water would back through the lower drains and fill three streets. The hidden spillway could divert it, but opening the access would destroy the cellar wall, undermine two storage bays, and probably ruin number five above them.

On the final page she had listed three warning signs: dark water at the bakery drain, vibration under Rookglass House, a wet diagonal fracture in the eastern foundation.

Two were already beneath my feet.

My telephone rang before I could search for the third. A breathless voice from the bakery asked whether Evadne was with me. Black water had come up through their floor.

Downstairs, the cellar crack opened with a noise like a branch splitting. Water slapped across the tiles.

Evadne looked at me.

“Ask,” I said.

“Leonie Sayer, will you open the east wall?”

The easy sale of the apartment ended in that question. So did the fantasy that I could pack my grandmother into six boxes and be finished with every choice she had made.

“Not until everyone hears the truth,” I said. “No inherited debt. No punishment for refusal. And when tonight is over, you close every line, including the ones people decline.”

“Some will refuse if they know they can.”

“Then ask for what you need, not what their grandparents offered.”

Water covered the soles of our boots.

Evadne held out her hand. “Agreed.”

I did not take it. “No promise. Just get them here.”

The residents of Mirehaven filled the entrance hall in twenty minutes. Some arrived because Evadne called. More came because their parents had taught them never to ignore a summons from number six. They brought the things their households had preserved against an unnamed day: pry bars wrapped in oilcloth, old iron keys, coils of rope, shovels, a masonry drill, a hand winch. One driver parked a recovery truck outside. Another came with a van to move people from the lower streets.

They watched Evadne. Evadne watched me.

So I told them.

I showed them the ledger and the plans. I told them the promise-working kept Evadne young and trapped, not them obedient. No ancestor's consent had entered their blood. Anyone could leave. Anyone who left would lose nothing except the chance to help keep black water out of their neighbors' homes.

An elderly woman in a green raincoat began to cry. “My mother said our family would sicken if we refused.”

“Your mother was mistaken,” Evadne said.

“You never corrected her.”

“No.”

The woman set down the case of tools she had brought. “Then I refuse you.”

A murmur moved through the hall.

Evadne opened the ledger, found the line the woman indicated, and drew her pen through it. “Released,” she said.

The woman stared, perhaps waiting for a pain that did not come. Then she picked up the case again.

“These aren't for you,” she said. “My daughter lives downhill.”

“Understood.”

That was the moment the room changed. Not into bravery; there was too much weather beating at the doors for that. But fear loosened its grip enough for decisions to fit beside it.

Evadne asked the hardware household for their kept key to open the rear service gate. She asked the mechanic to anchor the winch outside. She asked the bakery family for every empty flour sack they could fill with rubble. She asked two households for evacuation vehicles, four for strong backs, one for knowledge of the old drains. Each time she asked, she waited for an answer. Some said no. She released them. Enough said yes.

Then she turned to me.

I took up my grandmother's mason's hammer.

The plaster broke easily. The brick behind it did not. We worked knee-deep in water while the drill screamed and grit coated our mouths. When we had opened a hole wide enough to see through, my torch found a stone gallery packed with branches, silt, and pieces of a collapsed iron screen. A wheel taller than I was stood on the far side, red with rust.

Another surge struck. The hole spat water hard enough to knock a man backward.

Evadne stepped into it.

She planted both hands on the broken edges of the wall and spoke words too low for me to understand. Pale light spread from her palms through the mortar, branching like roots under ice. The stones stopped shifting. She did not. Her shoulders shook with every impact from the water.

“I can hold the passage,” she said through her teeth. “I cannot open it.”

We widened the breach around her. The mechanic fed the winch cable through and hooked the fallen screen. Upstairs, the truck's engine roared. Iron shrieked along stone. Others dragged out branches and shoveled silt into flour sacks, passing them hand to hand toward the rear gate.

The wheel would not move.

I climbed through with my grandmother's plans inside my coat. Water reached my thighs, then my waist as the gallery dipped. Behind me, Evadne's light showed each crack she held shut. Ahead, the spillway gate shuddered in its frame.

The diagram showed a retaining catch on our side. I found it under the water, drove a chisel beneath it, and struck until my wrist went numb. The catch lifted. The wheel turned a quarter circle and stopped.

The gallery lurched.

One of Evadne's hands tore free of the wall. A seam opened overhead, pouring gravel and water. The people behind me scattered; then two came back to brace Evadne's arm while she pressed her palm into place again. The light returned, dimmer.

“There is another keeper,” I shouted.

My grandmother had drawn it on the far side of the gate.

The only way to reach it was through a maintenance gap barely wider than my shoulders. Water hammered through it. Someone tied a rope around my waist. Evadne looked at the plan, then at me.

“Your grandmother intended to do this herself.”

“She should have written better instructions.”

I went through before I could become sensible.

Cold closed over my head. For a few seconds there was no town, no inheritance, only stone scraping my coat and the rope cutting under my ribs. I pulled myself into the pocket beyond the gate and came up coughing in darkness.

The second keeper was above me, furred with rust. I fitted the chisel. My first blow glanced away. My second rang through the metal. On the third, the keeper dropped.

“Turn it!” I yelled.

The wheel groaned. The gate climbed.

Water seized my legs and dragged me toward the opening. The rope snapped taut. Hands hauled from the other side while the river battered through, carrying years of silt with it. I lost the hammer. I kept the plans inside my coat.

Then the spillway took the surge.

The water changed direction with a deep, bodily roar. It rushed away beneath the hill toward the marsh instead of forcing itself back under the lower streets. The pressure fell. One by one, the cracks around Evadne's hands went dark.

We crawled from the cellar near dawn, soaked black to the shoulders and gray with brick dust. Rookglass House had lost part of its east foundation. Number five would not be sold in two days, or two months. But when the drivers returned from below, they reported wet floors, frightened residents, and no drowned streets.

Evadne sat on the bottom stair with the ledger open on her knees.

Those who had answered stood before her while she recorded what they had freely done and crossed out each line. For those who had refused, she wrote *released*. She did not hurry. The last open promise belonged to my grandmother.

Evadne offered me the pen.

“It was never mine,” I said.

“No.” She looked at the broken wall. “But the choice was.”

She wrote *released by death* beside my grandmother's promise. Beneath it, she added, *answered freely by Leonie Sayer*, and closed the book.

Nothing flashed. No wind swept the cellar. Evadne simply bowed her head as if listening to a sound recede.

In the washed blue light after the storm, half the town walked with her to the boundary marker. Perhaps they wanted to see whether she had lied. From the care with which Evadne placed each boot, I thought she wanted to know too.

Evadne stopped with one boot in Mirehaven and one beyond it. She looked suddenly uncertain, younger in that instant than her unchanged face had ever made her seem.

Then she stepped across.

No force pulled her back. She walked twenty paces down the wet road, laughing once under her breath. When she turned, a single silver hair shone beside her temple.

I thought of number five with its cracked floor and ruined sale. I thought of the city train leaving that afternoon, and of how easily a new duty could disguise itself as a choice. I did not decide my whole life beside a boundary stone.

I decided the morning.

“Evadne,” I called. “I have tea upstairs, if the kettle still works.”

She touched the silver hair, then looked back at Rookglass House.

“What will I owe you?”

“Nothing,” I said. “It's tea.”

She crossed into Mirehaven again because she wanted to, and came home with me through the rain.

stories.title: The Thousandth Fall
stories.prompt: - A monk uncovers The Wrong Way to Use Healing Magic and now, he trains beyond human limitations, using his self-healing abilities to gain absurd strength, unrivaled stamina, and insane speed.
stories.body:
# The Thousandth Fall

The litter reached the monastery after midnight, with rainwater running from its poles and four exhausted novices stumbling beneath it. Cavori took the front before anyone asked. The climb had emptied the bearers. It had not emptied him.

He carried the injured traveler up the last three flights of cliff stairs at a run.

In the infirmary, the monks cut away a trouser leg black with mud. The traveler's boot had twisted backward beneath a fallen cart, and the cold had worked into him during the slow ascent. Cavori stood ready beside the cot, breathing hard, his palms shining with the faint amber light of his gift. He could close the split skin on his own shoulder where the litter pole had rubbed it raw. He could quiet the strain in his back and make his lungs stop burning. He could not turn that light outward.

By dawn, the infirmarian had saved the traveler's life but not his crushed foot.

“If we'd reached him sooner,” Cavori said.

The infirmarian washed blood and road grit from her hands. “Then we would have had more choices.”

It was not blame. Cavori received it as a task.

The storm worsened after sunrise. Wind pried a slate from the infirmary roof, then three more. Water sheeted down an interior wall. They were shifting the patients when a roof brace cracked above the center aisle.

Cavori heard it before he saw it: a splintering groan, deep enough to feel in his teeth. He lunged beneath the beam and caught it.

The weight drove him to one knee.

Someone shouted. The remaining slates sagged overhead. Cavori put both hands under the wet timber and pushed while the infirmarian shepherded patients toward the door. His shoulders flared with pain. Something inside his left arm gave a sickening little pull.

Amber light rose over his skin.

His gift usually answered injury after the harm was done. This time he did not release the beam. The magic closed what the load tore, and the load tore it again. Heat poured through him in waves. Each breath scraped; each breath cleared. He rose from his knee.

“Last one!” the infirmarian called.

Cavori held until the final cot passed outside. Then he threw himself aside. The brace struck the flagstones hard enough to crack one.

He lay listening to the roof settle. His arms trembled, but they did not feel ruined. They felt frighteningly ready.

When he stood, he gripped the fallen beam. It should have taken six monks and a lever to move. Cavori lifted one end clear of the floor by himself.

The infirmarian stared at the space beneath it. “Put that down.”

He did, carefully. “I think I healed wrong.”

The abbot heard his account in the rain barrel room because it was the only dry chamber not filled with patients. Cavori demonstrated with a stone grain weight that had defeated him since his novitiate. He lifted it, let strain gather, and called his magic without ending the effort. The amber glow came. The ache remained, but the weakness receded. When the light faded, he shifted the weight to one hand.

The abbot's face remained still. The infirmarian's did not.

“Healing returns the body to itself,” she said. “Yours has decided this is itself now.”

“Then I can change what it returns to.” Cavori heard the wonder in his voice and did not try to hide it. “I could have carried that traveler from the lower road alone. I could have been there before the cold set in.”

“You could also have broken beneath the beam,” the abbot said.

“But I didn't.”

“Pain warns you to stop. You have found a way to keep moving after the warning while the danger continues. That is the wrong way to use a mercy.”

Cavori looked at the weight balanced in his hand. “Is it wrong if it gets me there in time?”

The abbot considered him for so long that the rain seemed to fill the room. At last he allowed trials, bounded by witnesses, food, sleep, and the infirmarian's right to end any session. Cavori agreed before the conditions were finished.

They began with the cliff stairs.

He climbed until his legs failed, keeping the amber warmth moving through them. The first time, he stumbled at the seventieth step and struck the wet stone. The infirmarian made a mark in a ledger.

“Why record that?” he asked.

“Because you will remember the ascent and forget the fall.”

On the next climb he passed the seventieth step without slowing. He reached the upper gate, ran down, and climbed again.

The ledger gave him an idea he mistook for humility. He cut a tally into the practice-yard wall for every genuine collapse, every lost footing, every moment his body would have stopped without his gift. If there were a thousand marks and he still stood, he thought, no one could call the method reckless.

At first the gains came in small astonishments. A water jar felt lighter. The stair landings arrived sooner than expected. He could hold healing through an entire morning instead of losing focus after a few breaths.

Then the astonishments grew.

He shouldered a stone lintel while the masons reset its supports. He ran beside a supply cart when its brake failed, passed it on the downhill road, and reached the bend with time to drag a timber across the track. He carried two full water barrels up the cliff stairs, one under each arm, without spilling enough to wet his sandals. The amber light ceased to flicker. It became a steady radiance, as constant as his pulse.

His speed multiplied with his strength. Every repaired stride began where the last impossible stride had ended. Soon novices heard the slap of his sandals on the lowest stair and turned to find him already at the gate. Soon he could sprint to the valley floor and return before the kitchen bell finished calling the community to breakfast.

His stamina became harder to measure. He moved stones all afternoon after running since dawn, took an evening watch for a feverish brother, then joined the bakers before sunrise because carrying flour no longer tired him. He accepted every request with relief. A burden carried was a danger someone else did not have to face.

If he sat still, though, the old night returned: the litter poles slick beneath his hands, the injured traveler shivering while the stairs delayed them. Cavori had begun training because one person had needed him sooner. He continued because stopping felt too much like consenting to the next late arrival.

The monastery adjusted around him. A cracked cistern needed lifting? Send Cavori. A novice had left medicine at a roadside shelter? Cavori could fetch it before the kettle boiled. Three crews were needed to clear stormfall? One monk would do.

The infirmarian still ordered rest. Cavori learned to appear restful. He sat cross-legged in the courtyard while sustaining the warm current beneath his robe. He reported soreness but not how quickly it vanished. He ate the prescribed meals, then trained while others slept.

The marks accumulated: three hundred; six hundred; nine hundred.

He stopped asking why each task was his. That seemed less important than the fact that he could finish it. When other monks reached for a load, he was already lifting. When they tied ropes, he trusted his hands instead. He did not notice how often help arrived after he had made it useless.

Fall nine hundred ninety-nine came in an empty practice yard at dusk. Cavori leaped from the parapet, landed badly on purpose, and caught himself with one hand. Amber light flashed. Stone dust burst beneath his palm.

He rose to make the mark and found the abbot standing beside the wall.

The old tally cuts made a rough gray field. The newest gleamed white.

“You dismissed your witness three hours ago,” the abbot said.

“The session ended. This was one jump.”

“It was one lie.”

Cavori placed the chisel at the next empty space. “Tomorrow I'll take the thousandth fall with the whole monastery watching. Then we can stop pretending I am one bad step from disaster.”

“Nine hundred ninety-nine falls prove that your flesh can close around nine hundred ninety-nine mistakes.”

“They prove more than that.”

“Not that your judgment heals. Not that your attention is endless. Not that every burden belongs to you.”

Cavori drove the chisel harder than necessary. “The traveler on the storm road did not need my judgment. He needed me to be faster.”

“And now you believe every suffering person needs you first.”

“If I can reach them first, why shouldn't I?”

“Because speed is not permission. Because strength is not wisdom. Because if you make yourself into a tool, eventually everyone here will learn to use you like one.”

The road answered with a sound like distant thunder.

Both men turned.

Along the outer wall, warning bells began to ring. A novice on the gate tower pointed down the cliff. The rain-softened road had broken beneath a returning party of pilgrims and their escorts. A slab of earth was sliding toward the lower bend, gathering stones and uprooted brush. Figures scattered before it.

Cavori dropped the chisel.

The abbot caught his sleeve. For one sharp instant Cavori expected an order to stay.

“Find them,” the abbot said. “We will bring ropes.”

Cavori ran.

The gate vanished behind him. Stairs blurred into a gray ribbon beneath his feet. He passed the first tumbling stones, then the dust front, then the leading edge of the slide itself. Gravel hissed around his ankles. He ran faster.

At the lower bend, six pilgrims were staring uphill, frozen by the moving earth.

“Into the trees!” Cavori shouted.

One man pointed to an overturned handcart. An older pilgrim lay pinned beneath its axle. The hillside buckled fifty paces away.

Cavori lifted the cart with one hand, gathered the injured pilgrim with the other, and carried him to the trees. He went back for the man who had stopped to help, then for a novice whose ankle would not bear weight. On his fourth crossing, the landslide swallowed the bend.

It did not catch him.

He ran uphill through the boiling dust, carrying two people. Stones struck his back and bounced away. The amber light poured from his arms and legs, mending each blow while his stride continued. He left the pilgrims above the break and raced down again before the stones he had dislodged reached the road.

There was no pause in him now, no shortening stride or desperate reserve saved for later. He made the ruined distance six more times while the cliff continued to move. He bore an injured pilgrim uphill, returned for packs containing medicine and blankets, then returned again because a novice swore someone had called from the dust. Cavori searched every ditch and splintered cart until he found the missing woman already climbing with another pilgrim's arm around her. He did not take her away. He matched their pace until they reached firm ground, then vanished downhill once more.

The remaining novices had taken shelter on a narrow section of paving that jutted from the cliff. A stone span connected it to stable ground. As Cavori reached them, the span cracked across its middle.

He caught the falling half on his shoulders.

For an instant the world became weight. Blocks the size of grain chests pressed him knee-deep into mud. The broken paving trembled behind him, holding three novices and a pilgrim above a steep drop.

Cavori straightened.

Stone ground against stone. Amber light shone through the rain in sheets. He raised the span until its upper surface met the stranded section, making a crooked bridge of his back and the ruin he carried.

“Cross,” he said.

The youngest novice crawled toward him and stopped. “Brother, it will crush you.”

“It is trying.” Cavori set his feet deeper. “Go.”

The pilgrim crossed first, dragging one leg. Then one novice, then another. Cavori felt each footstep through the slab. He heard the rescue party arriving above: the abbot calling positions, the infirmarian demanding anchor knots, a dozen voices answering.

The youngest novice remained. The paving beneath him tore loose.

He fell without a sound.

Cavori's body gathered itself to follow. For months, that had been enough: see a burden, become the answer. But he still held a broken road above three rescuers edging down with ropes. If he released it too early, his speed would save one person and bury the rest.

“Take the weight!” he shouted.

Ropes dropped around the span. Hands hauled them taut. Cavori waited until he felt the pull settle through every line.

Then he let go and jumped.

The novice tumbled below him, robe snapping in the wind. Cavori drove himself from the cliff face, struck a spur of rock, and leaped again. He fell faster than gravity could take the boy.

He caught him just above a lower ledge.

Cavori twisted so his own back met the stone. The impact emptied the world of light and sound.

Then the amber glow returned.

It moved slowly at first, warm through the crushing dark. Breath came back. Rain touched his face. The novice was curled safely against his chest, sobbing hard enough to shake them both.

High above, the ropes held. The rescuers had the broken span. No second collapse came roaring after them.

Cavori looked up the cliff at the tally wall he could not see.

“One thousand,” he whispered.

The number felt nothing like proof.

He could have climbed out carrying the novice. His fingers already found holds in the slick rock; his legs had strength enough. But a rescue rope descended, knocking pebbles from the ledge, and the infirmarian's voice followed it.

“Secure the boy first!”

Cavori obeyed. He tied the novice into the waiting sling and watched the others raise him. When the rope returned, Cavori fastened it around himself.

“I can climb,” he called.

The abbot leaned over the edge, rain streaming from his hood. “We can pull.”

Cavori considered refusing. Then he sat back in the harness and let the community lift him.

They fed him in the infirmary after the injured were settled. The amber light had repaired what the fall had done, but the infirmarian examined him anyway. Cavori answered every question. He drank the bitter broth she put in his hands. He slept until the next afternoon.

When he woke, the abbot was seated beside the cot with the fall ledger closed on his lap.

“Will you forbid it?” Cavori asked.

“Would you obey?”

Cavori thought of secret midnight climbs and pain converted into numbers. “Not a simple prohibition.”

“Then we require a wiser rule than either of us brought to the practice yard.”

They made one before Cavori stood: no unwitnessed training, no hidden healing, no task assigned to him merely because he could endure it, and no assumption that another body would answer magic as his did. The infirmarian retained the right to stop him. Cavori gained the right to refuse.

They left the thousand marks in the wall, not as instruction but as warning.

The next morning, Cavori returned to the broken road. A rescue stone still blocked the path, broad enough that the work crew had set rollers and three hauling ropes around it. He could have thrown it into the ravine. Instead he crouched, lifted just enough for the others to slide the first roller underneath, and held it there.

Amber light gathered around his hands. The stone weighed less than the breakfast tray had once weighed.

“Ready,” called a novice at the ropes.

Cavori waited until every worker had found footing.

“Together,” he said.

stories.title: There Goes Your Name
stories.prompt: "There goes your name" the fae cooed. "Now, go ahead and pick a new one!" name magic is over rated anyways...
stories.body:
# There Goes Your Name

The payment came out through my mouth, though I did not speak.

One moment my name lived where it always had, fastened behind my teeth and under my ribs, threaded through every time my mother had called me in from rain. The next, the fae hooked one green fingernail beneath my lower lip and drew out a filament of gold.

It did not hurt. That frightened me more than pain would have.

The thread kept coming. It whispered across my tongue, carrying voices with it: my father laughing as he taught me to whistle, my brother shouting for me from the top of the pear tree, my own voice given back by a well. The memories stayed. Only their address went sliding away.

At last the thread came free. The fae wound it twice around one long finger. A brightness pulsed there in the damp orchard house, small and warm as a vein beneath skin.

“There goes your name,” the fae cooed. “Now, go ahead and pick a new one!”

Across the room, the cage opened.

It was not a cage anyone had built. Apple branches had grown through the floorboards and bent together around my brother, their twigs interlaced so tightly that not even his hand could pass between them. Now they unknitted with the dry, deliberate sound of fingers snapping. He stumbled out, one cheek patterned red from bark and his hair full of dead petals.

I caught him before he fell.

He gripped the front of my coat. “Is it you?”

“Yes.” My answer came at once. My voice was mine. The scar on his chin was the one he had earned at six, chasing me over a stone wall. I knew he hated cooked carrots, lied badly, and slept with both feet outside the blanket. I knew I had found his empty bed three nights ago and followed apple blossoms through a winter field to this house.

I knew I would do it again.

His shoulders loosened. He pressed his face against me, just once, then pulled back as if embarrassed by the need. He was young enough to be frightened and old enough to resent being seen frightened.

Behind him, the fae flicked my name-thread over its knuckle.

Something in me turned toward the glint. Not my body. Not even my attention, exactly. It felt like hearing someone call from another room and knowing, after one startled heartbeat, that they meant somebody else.

The gate stood open beyond the orchard house. I could see it through the crooked doorway: two stone posts, a black iron arch, and between them the pale field under a sinking moon. We had only to cross it. That had been the bargain.

“His freedom,” I said, tightening my arm around my brother, “for my name. Paid and finished.”

“Paid,” said the fae. “Certainly.”

It moved between us and the door.

The orchard house smelled of wet plaster and fruit left too long in a cellar. Roots buckled the floor. Shelves sagged under brown jars in which moth wings, milk teeth, and little folded shadows floated in cloudy liquid. The fae seemed the only clean thing there. Its pale coat had pearl buttons. Its silver-green hair lay smooth against its narrow skull. Even its bare feet were free of mud.

It smiled at my brother, who stepped behind me.

“But your elder has a difficulty,” it said. “One cannot go about being called nothing. Think of the inconvenience.”

“Move,” I said.

“Gladly, as soon as the choosing is done.”

From inside its sleeve, the fae produced a fan of slips thin enough for light to shine through. Each was the brown-green of an apple leaf after frost. Ink curled across them, but whenever I tried to read a word, I heard it instead.

Brave, said one in the voice of a crowd.

Beloved, breathed another beside my ear.

Fortunate chimed like coins poured onto a table.

My brother stared. “Take one.”

From the bottom of every slip ran a hair-fine green strand. The strands gathered between the fae’s fingers and disappeared into its cuff.

“Not yet,” I said.

“We need to go.” His voice cracked on the last word. Outside, the black branches shifted although there was no wind. Beyond the gate, the field waited, ordinary and cold.

“We will.”

The fae extended the fan. “Bravery would suit. You displayed some in coming here.”

“If I choose it, what must I do?”

“Do?” The fae widened its amber eyes. “Why, you must be brave.”

“For whom?”

“What an anxious question.”

“Who decides whether I have been?”

The fan snapped shut. “Names decide many things for themselves.”

That was not an answer, and the fae knew I knew it. Its smile remained, but the corners sharpened.

I nodded at the second slip. “And beloved?”

“A comfort for a lonely soul.”

“Whose love?”

“Must you inspect every gift for thorns?”

“In this orchard?”

For the first time, its smile disappeared.

My brother tugged my sleeve. His fingers were icy. “Please. Any one. You can change it later.”

The fae’s pleasant expression returned. “Listen to him. Such good sense in a little thing.”

I looked again at the green strands. When the fae shifted its wrist, the slips shifted with it, though the air was still. My old name lay wound in gold around its other hand. The prepared names were not gifts. They were reins with pretty words painted on them.

I could have chosen one anyway. The gate was twenty paces off. I could have worn a new tether long enough to get my brother through, then fought whatever followed outside. That thought had the clean shape of desperation. It asked me to forget that the fae had taken him from his bed without opening a window and grown a prison around him in less than three days.

I needed to know what remained mine.

I touched the notch in my brother’s chin. “You got this jumping the wall behind the mill.”

He blinked. “What?”

“You cried because you tore your good trousers, not because you were bleeding. I gave you mine to tie around your knee. Then I told Father a dog had stolen them off the washing line.”

“He didn’t believe you.”

“No. He made me scrub both pairs.”

The memory was intact: soap numbing my hands, my brother sitting on an upturned bucket to keep me company, both of us choking back laughter whenever Father passed the washroom. Yet when I reached for the sound Father had used to scold me, I found a bright distance. I could remember being called. I could remember answering. The call itself led elsewhere, down a road of gold to the fae’s curled finger.

Grief rose so quickly that I had to grip my brother’s shoulder to stay upright.

The fae saw. “There now. You feel the hollow.”

“I feel the loss.”

“A hollow, precisely. Choose, and I shall fill it.”

“No.” I drew a breath that tasted of damp apples. “I chose to come after him. I chose the bargain. I choose to leave.”

“You have no name with which to choose.”

“You just called me ‘you.’”

The fae’s eyes narrowed.

I pressed on because irritation was safer than grief. “You called me his elder. A lonely soul. The one who came here. You have plenty of ways to describe me, but that doesn’t make any of them yours.”

“Cleverness is a poor coat in winter.”

“Still my coat.”

My brother made an impatient sound. “I know who you are.”

The words went through me more cleanly than comfort would have. He was not trying to solve me. He was tired, cold, and angry that anyone thought he might mistake me.

The fae studied us both. Its gaze stopped pretending to be kind.

“Then go,” it said.

It stepped aside.

I did not move.

The doorway beyond it was clear, but the orchard had changed while we talked. Thorny whips had crept across the path. They lay slack among the weeds, thin enough to step over, each hooked with backward-pointing barbs. At the gate, a living briar as thick as my wrist had braided itself between the stone posts. It passed through an iron ring and doubled back, a green-black latch furred with thorns.

Beside the orchard-house door hung a pruning hook. Its wooden handle was spotted with rot, but the curved blade showed a bright edge where years of use had worn it smooth.

“We can’t,” my brother whispered.

“The exchange is completed,” I said to the fae. “Open the gate.”

“The gate is not part of our exchange.”

“You said he would be free.”

“And so he is. See how no branch confines him.”

The thorns on the path began to lift.

Courtesy had been another latch. The fae had waited for me to choose a prepared name because that would look like agreement. Now that I would not, it was willing to let the orchard do what its spoken bargain could not.

My brother’s breath came fast against my shoulder. I put my hand over his where it clutched my coat.

“When I take the hook,” I said quietly, “stay behind me. Step where I step.”

The fae sighed. “Must rescue always make people tedious?”

“You could try being rescued.”

I lunged for the wall.

The fae was quicker. Its hand closed around my wrist before my fingers reached the hook. The touch was dry and cold. My brother struck at its arm. A root ripped up through the floor between his boots and flung him backward.

I drove my shoulder into the fae. It barely shifted. Up close, its amber eyes held black flecks that moved like ants. My stolen name warmed on its finger.

The fae smiled again, breath sweet with rotten fruit.

Then it spoke the name.

I will not set it down here. I could not if I wished to. I heard its shape clearly in that room, every sound polished by years of use, but none of it belonged to my mouth anymore.

“Kneel,” the fae commanded its owner. “Kneel and stay.”

I braced for my knees to buckle.

Nothing happened.

No, not nothing.

The gold thread jerked on the fae’s finger.

Its hand snapped downward, dragging my arm with it. The thread unwound in a bright rush, spilled across the floor, and darted through the doorway. It moved like a line pulled by an invisible needle. Over the lifted thorns, under a root, straight to the gate. There it looped around the heavy briar latch, dipped low to the earth, and knotted itself fast.

It knelt. It stayed.

The fae stared at the taut gold line between its hand and the gate.

I stared too.

It had not taken me. It had taken the part of the world that answered when that sound was used. A handle, severed and held. When the fae pulled on it, the handle moved.

The door had come off the bucket, and I was still standing.

My brother recovered first. He scrambled up and seized the pruning hook from the wall.

“That belongs here,” the fae said.

“So do the thorns.” He shoved the handle at me. “Do something.”

I took it.

The fae released my wrist and clawed at the gold around its finger. The knot at the gate held. The thread would not slip free, obedient to the last command.

I swung the hook low. The blade caught the first thorn-whip and pinned it against the floor. “Behind me.”

My brother stepped into the place I cleared. We moved out of the house. The orchard woke around us. Branches bowed over the path. Barbs scraped my boots and snagged my coat. I used the hook as a lever, forcing the worst of them aside, but every step let the last one spring back behind us.

The fae followed as far as the doorway, one arm stretched toward the gate by the golden thread.

“You cannot leave that behind,” it called. Its voice had lost its coo. “It is you.”

A thorn caught my sleeve and tore the cloth from wrist to elbow. I ripped free.

“It was mine,” I said. “There’s a difference.”

At the gate, the briar latch remained woven through the iron ring. Gold bound its middle, but kneeling had only bent it lower. It still barred the gap between the posts.

My brother grabbed it with both hands. The thorns bit his palms. He hissed and held on.

The fae pulled at the thread. The briar groaned but did not shift.

I understood what I needed before I understood whether it would work.

I turned my back to the gate and faced the fae. “You wanted me to come to you.”

Its lips parted.

“You brought my brother here because you knew I would follow. You made all those lovely names because you wanted me tethered. Are you going to let a stolen word refuse you now?”

The gold line trembled.

The fae’s face changed. Anger stripped it of elegance. For a heartbeat it looked as neglected as the orchard: skin grey as old wood, hair hanging in mossy ropes, mouth a crack in bark.

It spoke the old name again.

“Come to me!”

The thread obeyed.

Gold snapped back toward the fae’s hand. Because it had knotted itself around the briar, it took the latch with it. The living bar wrenched sideways through the iron ring. Its thorns shrieked against stone. The fae tried to release the line, but the loose coils wound over its palm and around its wrist, binding its reaching arm to the command.

The gate opened the width of a body.

I jammed the pruning hook into the mass of brambles and leaned with all my weight. The handle bowed. Thorns pressed close enough for me to smell their green sap.

“Through!”

My brother squeezed between the stone post and the dragged latch. His coat snagged. He tore it loose and tumbled onto the pale grass beyond.

The fae shouted my lost name a third time, followed by words I did not hear. The thread convulsed. The briar thrashed against the hook.

I let go.

The handle flew from my hands. I threw myself through the gap as the latch slammed back. A thorn raked my boot sole. Then I was on the other side, rolling down the shallow ditch, with my brother’s arms locked around my shoulders.

The moon vanished behind a bank of cloud.

For a few breaths, neither of us moved. Frost silvered the rough grass. The field smelled of mud and distant chimney smoke. No branches reached for us. The gate stood shut above the ditch, its arch framing darkness too dense to show the orchard house.

The fae came to the threshold but did not cross. Gold tethered its wrist to the briar latch. Its pale coat hung open now, stained at the hem, and leaf-thin names circled it in a restless flock.

“Come back,” it said. “Choose, and I will return what you threw away.”

“You pulled it out of me.”

“You offered it.”

That was true. I had offered it when the cage tightened around my brother and the fae asked what I would give. The choice had been mine, though the cruelty of it belonged elsewhere.

“I paid,” I said. “Keep your purchase.”

Its bound hand closed over the golden thread. “You will miss it.”

“I already do.”

The answer seemed to trouble it more than defiance. Perhaps it understood bargains only when people pretended not to care about the price.

My brother sat up beside me. Blood marked his palms in narrow lines. He looked at the fae, then at me, and said my old name once.

The sound crossed the gate.

It did not touch me. It entered the orchard and shivered along the gold until the thread brightened in the fae’s fist. I remembered my mother bending over a cradle. I remembered chalking those letters badly on a slate. I remembered my brother shortening the name when he wanted a favor and stretching it into three accusing syllables when I stole food from his plate.

I remembered whom it had meant.

Then the gold dimmed, and the address ended on the wrong side of the gate.

My brother’s mouth twisted. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be.” My throat ached. “I wanted to hear it from you once.”

Behind the gate, the first grey light seeped between the trees. The fae stepped backward. Branches closed over it, over the ruined coat and the fistful of names, until there was only an orchard going quietly to rot.

We walked until the gate was out of sight.

At the field’s edge we found a dry ditch beneath a hawthorn hedge. My brother sat with his back against the bank while I wrapped his palms with strips from my torn sleeve. Dawn spread slowly, revealing mud on our clothes, burrs in his hair, and a purple bruise along my wrist where the fae had held me. Ordinary injuries. I was grateful for every one.

When I finished the knots, my brother flexed his fingers.

“What am I supposed to call you?” he asked.

I had been waiting for the question. It still frightened me.

I tried a few sounds under my breath. One was too hard, a stone knocking against teeth. Another reminded me of the fae’s leaf-slips though I could not have said why. A third felt borrowed from somebody glimpsed across a market. None carried a thread. None carried anything.

Not yet.

My brother waited. For once, he did not rush me.

The sky above the hedge had turned the silver-blue that comes just before sunrise. A word occurred to me, assembled from no prophecy and promised by no whisper. I said it once to hear its weight.

“Sivren.”

My brother considered it with the grave suspicion he usually reserved for new food. “Sivren.”

No light flared. No hidden branch bent. Somewhere beyond the field, a cart rattled over a rough road.

“Do you like it?” he asked.

“I think I might.” The loss inside me had not closed. I did not want it to, not that morning. “It’s mine to offer, anyway.”

He pushed himself to his feet and held out one bandaged hand. “Come on, Sivren. We’re going home.”

I took it, and went with him.

stories.title: The Night Harvest
stories.prompt: Out of the blue, monsters appeared in our world. They appear at night, never seem to run out. A whole industry to profit off their corpses start to appear. One day, odd people start to appear as well. They barely communicate, and only seem interested in fighting and kill these monsters.
stories.body:
# The Night Harvest

The scale tipped past three tonnes, and the intake crew cheered.

They had been cheering all night. Every truck that backed beneath the floodlights carried another heap of hooked limbs, plated hides, and pale eyes filmed over in death. The drivers leaned on their horns. The cutters banged knives against the steel tables. Above us, the refinery board advanced another bright digit toward the largest harvest since the monsters had first begun appearing.

I did not cheer. Three tonnes was a good load, but the carcasses had been stacked warm. Warm weight could hide gas pockets, gut water, even a live clutchling if the truck crew had been careless. My job was to make the number honest.

I climbed the inspection step and drove my probe between two slabs of black hide. The upper carcass sagged around it. Blue light leaked from a tear below the breastplate and shone through my glove.

“Grade two hide,” I called. “One intact lumen sac. Dock them for heat.”

The driver swore. The crew cheered anyway.

I entered the grade on my tablet. The refinery bought hide for armor laminate, bone for kiln additive, blood salts for battery paste, and the luminous organs for the oil burning in the floodlights overhead. Ten months earlier we had called all of it monster. Now there were price columns.

At the end of the entry, an overtime notice filled my screen. Four more hours at hazard rate, with the night-harvest bonus if we broke the record. I thought of my brother asleep in the chair beside his narrow bed because lying flat still hurt his mending ribs. I thought of the rehabilitation bill under the sugar jar and the day-shift vacancy my supervisor had promised to the grader with the best quarterly attendance.

I signed.

**KESSA MORREN: HAZARD RATE APPROVED**, the receipt said.

“Good choice,” my supervisor said behind me. He spoke quietly even when the yard roared, which made people lean close and listen. “A night like this could pay your rent.”

“It could pay one-third of a brace.”

“Then let’s hope the things keep coming.”

He meant it kindly. That was how far the year had carried us.

The next truck came through the south gate too fast.

Its left headlamp was gone. Claw marks had peeled the paint from the cab, and one rear tire flapped against the rim. The truck struck the guide rail, throwing sparks, and slewed across the receiving lane. Cutters scattered. The driver braked a handspan from the scale house.

Something moved beneath the chassis.

I saw a joint bend the wrong way, then a barbed leg shot out and caught the ankle of a cutter who had not run quickly enough. He fell, striking the concrete. The monster pulled itself forward under the axle. It was small for the harvest, no bigger than a workbench, but alive enough to open a mouth along its belly.

Before security raised their shock rifles, a figure dropped from the truck roof.

The stranger landed on one knee. Layers of dull cloth hid their body and most of their face. In both hands they held a narrow weapon like a spear with a broken crescent at its tip. They hooked the monster beneath its jaw, turned with its rush, and drove the point through the seam behind its head. The creature struck the concrete once. Then it folded.

The stranger freed the cutter’s boot, checked the man with a quick press of two fingers against his throat, and stood.

For a moment nobody moved. Then the driver began clapping. A few cutters joined him. We had all heard about these people. They had started appearing three weeks earlier, always after sunset, alone or in small groups. They killed monsters with tools no one had seen them carry in daylight. They ignored money. They rarely answered questions. By morning they were gone.

The stranger looked past the applause to our processing tanks.

Three round towers stood behind the intake hall. Veins of blue light trembled in their sight glasses as ground lumen tissue circulated through hot solvent. The stranger went rigid.

My supervisor stepped forward with both palms open. “You saved a worker. We can pay.”

The stranger did not look at him. They crouched beside the dead monster and cut a careful line under its breastplate. A pear-shaped organ slid into their gloved hand, faintly glowing. They pointed at it, then at our tanks.

“Yes,” my supervisor said. “We process those.”

The stranger slashed the organ in half.

Blue fluid hissed on the concrete. The cutters stopped clapping.

The stranger pointed from the ruined organ to the tanks again, then swept one hand across their throat.

Security took that for a threat.

Four guards closed around them. The stranger could have struck first. I had seen how quickly they moved. Instead they let the crescent spear fall and raised empty hands. Even when a guard shoved them against the scale-house wall, their gaze never left the pulsing blue tanks.

“Put them in the old tool cage,” my supervisor said. “Police can decide what that performance meant after dawn.”

As the guards led the stranger away, I saw two more still figures beyond the south fence, just outside the reach of our lamps. They watched their companion disappear into the intake hall. Neither approached.

Then a call came over the yard radio: three packs converging, perhaps sixty animals in all.

The record board flickered upward.

Management ordered every line to full output. More monsters meant more danger at the fences, they told us, and danger required brighter lamps. Brighter lamps required oil. By midnight, all three tanks were beating blue against the dark like enormous hearts.

The old tool cage stood beside my grading desk. We had emptied it when security needed somewhere to keep the first thieves who discovered that a jar of lumen concentrate was worth more than a week’s wages. The stranger sat inside with their wrists bound in front of them. Their hood had fallen back, revealing close-cropped dark hair and a pale lattice of scars along one temple. Nothing about their face told me where they had come from.

Each time the pumps thudded, their eyes lifted to the tanks.

I tried the questions everyone had tried on fighters before.

“Who are you?”

No answer.

“Where did you come from?”

Their gaze moved to mine and away.

“Do you understand me?”

They touched the floor between us. Then they pointed to the nearest tank and tapped the concrete in time with its pulse.

“You think it will explode?”

They shook their head sharply.

I tore the backing from a stack of grade labels and drew the best monster I could manage: too many legs, wide mouth, blue organ. The stranger watched. I drew an arrow from it to a tank.

They took the grease pencil through the bars. Beside my monster they drew small circles, a dozen of them, scattered across the label. Then they drew one large circle around the tank. From every small circle, they made a line pointing inward.

I thought I understood. “We bring the organs here.”

Again the sharp head shake. They tapped the small circles, pointed toward the outer wall, and made their fingers walk toward the large one.

Monsters coming to the refinery.

Of course they were. We killed them here. Floodlights washed half the district white, and trucks arrived trailing blood scent from every road. The stranger had drawn the obvious and expected me to mistake it for revelation.

They turned over the label. This time they drew the organ, the tank, and a jagged line between them. They held their fist closed, then slowly opened it, finger by finger. With the other hand, they pointed into the dark.

Something answered outside.

The cry began below hearing, a vibration in my teeth, before it rose into the sound of sheet metal dragged across stone. Other voices joined it from three sides of the yard.

The stranger tapped the tank drawing.

The nearest sight glass brightened with the next pump stroke.

The outer cries came back on the same beat.

I checked the line gauges. Pressure was stable. Temperature was four degrees above target but safe. The pulse should have been an effect of the pumps, nothing more.

On my screen, the outer motion sensors filled with amber marks.

“How do I prove it?” I asked.

The stranger flattened their palm over the drawing of the tank.

Shut it off.

My hazard bonus was posted beside the record tally. Under it, the day-shift opening waited behind quarterly figures. My brother’s last message sat unopened at the top of my tablet: *Don’t stay late because of me.*

The first pack hit the north fence.

Wire boomed. The guards fired from the catwalk, blue-white shocks flashing between the rails. Cutters dragged the latest truck inside and dropped armored shutters over the loading bays. In the control room, my supervisor ordered the brightness raised another ten percent.

The refinery board celebrated four hundred tonnes.

I told myself I was checking a blockage. Secondary line two had shown uneven feed all week. A sixty-second pause sat within my grader authority if foreign matter threatened a batch. I pressed the hold control.

One pump fell silent.

The corresponding tank dimmed from painful blue to the color of banked coals. Above it, two floodlights went out. Battery strips snapped on along the walls, colder and weaker but enough to see the lane.

At the west fence, a cluster of monsters had been climbing over one another to reach three guards on the catwalk. They stopped.

Not slowed. Stopped.

Heads lifted. Bodies turned. The nearest guard fired into an exposed flank, but the creatures ignored him. They dropped from the fence and streamed north, angling past people, trucks, and open pools of blood toward the still-throbbing main tank.

The stranger stood inside the cage. Bound hands gripped the bars.

My supervisor appeared at my shoulder. “Why is line two down?”

“Watch the west camera.”

“I asked you a question.”

“They turned when the pump stopped.”

He studied the feed for two seconds. Then he reached across me and entered his override code.

The pump hammered back to life.

Blue rose through the tank. The monsters running north veered as one and came back toward us.

“That can’t be scent,” I said.

“It can be twenty things. Heat. Vibration. Your timing. A pack response we don’t understand.” His voice remained low, but there was strain under it now. “What I do understand is that those lamps keep this yard alive.”

“The batteries held.”

“For emergency evacuation, not production. If we stop refining, we lose the lights. We lose tonight’s stock. Drivers stop collecting carcasses, cutters lose shifts, and your wages vanish with theirs. You want to explain that experiment to them?”

The main tank flared so bright its sight glass vanished in white.

At the far edge of the yard, beyond the north fence, the dark changed shape. Empty ground filled with low silhouettes. Some might have come from the drainage ditch or the buildings beyond. I could not see clearly enough to swear how they arrived. I could only watch a fresh wave rise and face the tanks.

The amber marks doubled on my screen.

“Correlation,” my supervisor said, but he did not look at me. “We need the lamps at full.”

The stranger struck the cage bars once with their bound hands.

Not at us. At the tanks.

I had spent ten months turning nightmares into grades. We weighed, priced, cut, cooked, and sold them until an endless attack looked like a supply chain. The monsters fed the tanks. The tanks called through the dark. More monsters came, and we called that a harvest.

I opened my brother’s message. Beneath the first line, he had written, *The brace can wait. Come home in one piece.*

I took the cage keys from the security hook.

My supervisor caught my wrist. “Think very carefully.”

“I have.”

“You open that door, you’re finished here.”

The day shift, the bonus, the insurance contribution: he laid them all between us without naming them.

I twisted free and unlocked the cage.

The stranger stepped out. I cut the binding at their wrists with my sample knife, then kicked their crescent spear across the floor. They caught it before it stopped sliding.

They did not threaten my supervisor. They pointed to the red containment control behind my desk.

“I know,” I said.

I broke the cover and pressed my palm to the switch.

Sirens rolled through the refinery. Armored collars began descending around the three tanks. The normal shutdown would have circulated the luminous stock until it cooled, but emergency containment drowned the hot lines in sealing foam and dropped shield plates around every storage vessel. It would spoil the batch and leave the pumps clogged solid. Once started, it required someone at the intake panel to hold the quench cycle until all three temperature bars reached black.

My supervisor slammed his badge against the cancel reader.

The collars stopped halfway.

“There are people on those walls,” he said. He pointed at the camera as monsters packed against the north gate. “You want to test a stranger’s drawing with their lives?”

“Restarting was the test.”

I shoved his badge away and hit containment again.

The main floodlights died.

Darkness seemed to drop with weight. People shouted. A cutter screamed that the fence had opened. Then battery bars glimmered along the lane, vehicle headlamps swung into place, and the yard returned in hard white fragments. It was less light than we were used to, but not none.

The stranger ran toward the north gate.

The two figures I had seen beyond the fence were already there. One carried a pair of short blades. The other swung a weighted cord that snapped tight around hooked legs and pulled monsters away from fleeing workers. None of the fighters pursued creatures that turned aside. They held the gap between the broken gate and the intake panel.

My supervisor lunged for the restart lever.

I planted both hands on it. He was stronger. The lever rose a notch, and deep under the floor one pump coughed.

Every monster at the gate surged.

The crescent spear flashed in the vehicle beams. Its wielder braced, turned one creature into another, and nearly went down beneath them. One of the companions hauled them free.

“Look,” I shouted.

My supervisor looked.

I bore down with all my weight. For one breath he resisted. Then a guard on the catwalk yelled for more battery lamps, and my supervisor’s grip loosened. I forced the lever into containment lock and drove my steel grading stamp through the locking eye.

The mechanism bit down on it. There would be no restart without cutting the panel apart.

“You’ve destroyed the line,” he said.

“Yes.”

Tank one went dark.

The quench control bucked under my palm. Heat warnings crawled across the screen. I could leave and let the automatic cycle fail, or stay until the stock was sealed. Foam burst from a joint overhead and pattered hot across my sleeve. I did not move my hand.

Tank two dimmed. Its pulse became a flutter.

Outside, the fighters gave ground one step at a time. Security had stopped aiming at them. Guards fired over their shoulders while cutters carried the injured into the scale house. My supervisor stood beside me, staring at the ruined controls and calling temperatures from the screen. Whether he was helping me or protecting what remained of his plant, I never asked.

“Third collar is sticking,” he said.

I leaned harder on the control. “Pressure?”

“Dropping. Hold it.”

The last tank beat once, bright enough to paint every face blue.

Then the collar closed.

The pulse stopped.

The monsters at the gate faltered. The fighters killed the three already inside the lane. No fresh bodies filled the spaces those creatures left.

Beyond the fence, the pack broke apart. Some fled into alleys and drainage cuts. Others turned their narrow heads toward the horizon, where a distant industrial glow stained the low clouds, and began moving that way. They did not vanish. They did not become harmless. But for the first time in months, the ground outside our refinery was not replacing them faster than we could count.

Nobody cheered.

At dawn, the managers gathered in the control room and began building their version of the night. A hostile stranger had sabotaged essential lighting. A panicked employee had released them. Unusual pack motion had followed a routine pressure fault. Operations would resume as soon as maintenance cleared the lines.

They forgot that graders are paid to keep numbers honest.

Every intake entry carried tank pressure, pump timing, yard video, and my authority code. I copied the sixty-second line test, the supervisor’s restart, the surge, and the full shutdown to my tablet. Then I sent it to the shift channel, the safety office, every local reporter whose address I could find, and my own private account.

By the time management disabled my access, the files had been forwarded hundreds of times. Before I left the yard, notices arrived that three other refiners using concentrated lumen stock had suspended their night runs pending investigation. No one promised the shutdowns would end the appearances. No one knew whether their plants would show the same pattern. But they were going to look.

The three fighters waited at the ruined gate.

The one I had freed touched the empty organ pouch on a dead monster, pointed at our shielded tanks, then toward the distant glow. The same warning, continued elsewhere.

“Is that why you came?” I asked. “Did you follow them? Did they follow you?”

Their face revealed nothing. They inclined their head to me once, turned, and walked into the paling dark with their companions.

I watched until the road hid them.

Then I went home unemployed, carrying a spoiled grading stamp and the smell of sealing foam. My brother was awake when I opened the door. He looked at the burns on my sleeve, then at my face, and did not ask about the bonus.

“Did they stop coming?” he asked.

“Not everywhere,” I said. “Maybe not even here.”

Behind me, the refinery floodlights remained dark. Morning had softened the windows, but it was the night ahead I imagined: battery lamps, shuttered tanks, no blue pulse beating a path toward our door.

I set the broken stamp beside the bills.

“Tonight,” I told him, “we find out what ordinary dark looks like.”

stories.title: The Vacant Throne
stories.prompt: Fifteen years ago, the human king and the demon queen fought a legendary battle that resulted in the king's death. The throne remained vacant until a half-demon child appeared bearing the royal sword.
stories.body:
# The Vacant Throne

The law allowed lost regalia through the throne-hall doors. It did not say what the guards should do when the person carrying it had horns.

By the time the fifteenth memorial bell stopped ringing, Rielle stood inside a cage of crossed pikes. The royal sword lay along her forearms, wrapped in dun wool and tied with a red cord. Hundreds of mourners packed the benches behind her. At the far end of the hall, the throne waited above eleven shallow steps, bare except for the old king’s circlet on its seat.

No monarch had touched either in fifteen years.

The guard at Rielle’s left stared at the blunt black tips of her horns. The guard at her right stared at the shape beneath the wool. Both had forgotten to take her name.

Rielle kept her thumbs away from the bundle. Her mother’s last instruction had concerned thumbs: *Keep yours loose when they crowd you. If it hooks the guard, you’ll draw before you decide.*

At the foot of the steps, Lord Protector Cadran Mirel folded the memorial proclamation he had been reading. He wore no crown, only a square silver seal at his throat, but everyone else watched him before deciding whether to breathe.

“Outer rank, bar the doors,” he said. “Inner rank, clear three paces around the claimant. Do not touch the bundle.”

That final order was the first thing about him Rielle liked.

White rods tapped shoulders as the inner guards pushed citizens back. The west doors shut easily. The east doors met the weight of people still crowding in from the square and stopped half a handspan short of their frame. Two guards leaned against them.

Cadran looked from the gap to Rielle. “You have interrupted the king’s remembrance. Name what you carry.”

Rielle had rehearsed a speech during twenty-three days of travel. The packed hall had boiled it down to one legal sentence.

“I petition an assay of lost regalia before the full council.”

The silver chains on the council benches rattled as people turned. A woman in black court wool rose from the first bench, tucking a writing board beneath one arm. Councilor Ysabet Roane was small, gray-haired, and already irritated.

“Who taught you that petition?” she asked.

“My mother.”

“Name her for the record.”

“Demon Queen Sarthene.”

Noise struck the hall like weather. A man behind Rielle shouted *murderer*. Someone farther back shouted for the doors to be opened. The east doors jumped in their frame as the crowd outside pushed again.

Cadran raised one hand. “If the object is what she implies, it is stolen royal property. Take her alive. Councilor, you may assay it once it is in our custody.”

Ysabet did not sit. “There is no royal custody while the throne is vacant. The claimant’s rail holds disputed regalia until provenance is heard.”

“I am the protector of the throne.”

“Clause nine lists the offices that may take custody. Yours is not among them.”

She spoke without heat, as if correcting a copied date. Four clerks hurried to lift two brass bars from grooves in the floor. They joined the bars with a crosspiece and spread a square of white linen over it, making a waist-high table between Rielle and the steps.

“Bearer,” Ysabet said, “place the object on the rail without uncovering it. State its keepers from the last acknowledged royal custody onward. Names and sequence. Leave motives out.”

Rielle stepped between the pikes. The wool dragged against her palms when she lowered the sword.

“King Veradan. Sarthene. Me.”

The hall found a new kind of silence.

Cadran’s gaze sharpened. “You omitted the thief between the king and the demon queen.”

“No.”

“Then say how she took it.”

Ysabet’s chalk clicked against her board. “Provenance first. Account second. Let her finish.”

“Sarthene kept it in a stone chest sealed with her own mark,” Rielle said. “She opened the chest in front of me twenty-four days ago. I cut her seal. I wrapped the sword. No one else has held it.”

“Did she order you here?”

The question came from Cadran, but Ysabet’s chalk waited for the answer.

“She forbade an escort across the border. She said an army would answer the question before I could.” Rielle looked at the linen instead of the throne. “She told me where the road ran. I chose it.”

“A child repeats the choice prepared for her.” Cadran turned so the benches, not Rielle, received his words. “Sarthene killed Veradan. She took his sword. Now, on the very day we mourn him, she sends us a horned claimant and calls the intrusion voluntary.”

He gave the hall a clean sequence. It was almost a relief to hear. Nothing in it required a person to wonder what a dying king might have done after the famous blow.

Ysabet held out a hand toward the bundle. “Untie the cord. Unwrap from your side. Touch no metal.”
